Learnable yet not simulable: a quantum resource theory of learning models

Xinbiao Wang1 Affiliation: 1College of Computing and Data Science, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore 639798, Singapore    Yuxuan Du1 Thanks: Correspondence to: duyuxuan123@gmail.com,
dacheng.tao@ntu.edu.sg Affiliation: 1College of Computing and Data Science, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore 639798, Singapore    Dacheng Tao1 Thanks: Correspondence to: duyuxuan123@gmail.com,
dacheng.tao@ntu.edu.sg Affiliation: 1College of Computing and Data Science, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore 639798, Singapore
Abstract

Quantum resource theory has sharpened our understanding of the intrinsic complexity of quantum systems, particularly their classical simulability. However, it remains unclear which quantum resource governs the classical learnability of quantum circuits, especially beyond the regime of efficient classical simulation. Here we close this knowledge gap by studying the expectation-value functions of families of tunable quantum circuits, with many applications in digital quantum simulation, quantum metrology, and quantum-system characterization. Specifically, we introduce a new resource measure, the dynamical stabilizer entropy (𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}), which quantifies how broadly an expectation-value function is distributed across its frequency modes. By relating 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} to operator stabilizer entropy, we establish a computational phase diagram that compares classical simulators with quantum-data-assisted classical surrogates. We first determine the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-dependent learnability boundary of this diagram by deriving bounds on the sample complexity and runtime of classical surrogates, and by developing a 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate. We then complete the diagram by proving, under standard complexity-theoretic assumptions, the existence of circuit families that can be efficiently learned by this surrogate but cannot be efficiently emulated from their circuit descriptions alone. Numerical experiments on random and structured circuits with up to 80 qubits support the predicted 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-dependent computational landscape. These results establish a quantitative resource-theoretic framework for delineating the boundary between classical simulation and learning, motivate resource measures linking quantum resources to learnability, and guide the design of learning-based algorithms for scalable quantum systems beyond the reach of direct classical simulation.

I Introduction

Quantum resources offer quantitative criteria for probing the intrinsic complexity of quantum systems, from characterization and algorithmic advantage to classical simulability [chitambar2019quantum]. Over the past decades, a broad range of such resources has been identified, with entanglement and magic serving as paradigmatic examples [horodecki2009quantum, bravyi2005universal, veitch2014resource, leone2025entanglement]. Together, these resources delineate whether quantum systems can be efficiently characterized through tasks such as tomography [leone2024learning, chia2024efficient, grewal2025efficient, mele2025efficient, mele2025learning] and fidelity estimation [Flammia201111dirct, leone2023nonstabilizerness, hinsche2025efficient], how quantum algorithms acquire provable advantages [takagi2019operational, takagi2019general, ahnefeld2022coherence, ahnefeld2026coherence], and whether concrete quantum problems remain accessible to classical methods [seddon2021quantifying, christandl2024resource, gu2025magic, zhang2025classical]. When the relevant resources are constrained, the corresponding systems can admit efficient classical simulation, as exemplified by tensor-network methods for limited entanglement [markov2008simulating, villalonga2019flexible, cirac2021matrix, pan2022simulation, berezutskii2025tensor] and near-Clifford or Pauli-based methods for restricted magic and operator structure [bravyi2016improved, bravyi2016trading, bravyi2019simulation, rudolph2023classical, beguvsic2024fast]. This resource-based perspective has become especially visible in recent experiments on quantum processors with tens to hundreds of qubits [kim2023evidence, google2025observation, fischer2026dynamical, tindall2026dynamics, haghshenas2026digital], where claims of quantum advantages are tested against classical simulators tailored to the structure of the problem being solved.

Beyond these established roles, quantum resources are beginning to reshape quantum learning [biamonte2017quantum, dunjko2018machine], a regime in which quantum systems and learning models become mutually enabling. Early studies have developed along two complementary directions. One asks how quantum resources control the expressivity, trainability, and generalization of quantum learning models [marrero2021entanglement, Holmes_2022, bu2022statistical, bu2023effects, Il_rio_Correr_2024, wang2024separable, bu2024complexity]. The other examines how resources enter the learning problem beyond the model itself, through entangled training data [schatzki2021entangled, Sharma_2022, wang2024transition], quantum access models or resourceful target distributions [Huang_2021, buadescu2021improved, aharonov2022quantum, chen2022exponential, huang2022quantum, hinsche2023one, fanizza2022learning, zhao2025entanglement]. However, unlike classical simulability, classical learnability still lacks a resource-theoretic characterization. Recent classical surrogates sharpen this gap [huang2021provably, schreiber2023classical, Sweke2025potential]. After consuming a limited number of quantum samples during training, they can later predict the behaviour of related quantum systems entirely on the classical side. Theoretical results show that such surrogates are provably efficient for circuit families with large non-Clifford content and substantial entangling structure, even when these same features make instance-wise classical simulation costly [du2025efficient, liao2025demonstration]. This fundamental difference raises a central question: What makes a quantum system learnable when it is not classically simulable?

In this study, we answer this question by establishing a computational phase diagram that delineates the capabilities of classical surrogates and classical simulators within a unified quantum resource framework, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Concretely, we consider the task of estimating expectation-value functions generated by NN-qubit quantum circuits containing dd tunable Pauli rotation gates. Such functions underpin a wide range of applications, ranging from digital quantum simulation [feynman2018simulating, zhang2022digital] and quantum metrology [degen2017quantum, koczor2020variational] to variational quantum algorithms [cerezo2021variational_VQA] and quantum-system certification [eisert2020quantum, Flammia201111dirct]. To characterize the learnability of these functions, we introduce a new resource measure ℳ\mathcal{M}, termed dynamical stabilizer entropy (𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}), which quantifies how broadly an expectation-value function is distributed across the frequency modes generated by the tunable gates.

We first use 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} to establish the information-theoretic boundary of classical learnability in the computational phase diagram. By deriving 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-dependent upper and lower bounds on the sample complexity, we show that the learnability of the explored circuit families ℱ𝒰λ\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}_{\lambda}} with bounded 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} ℳλ\mathcal{M}_{\lambda} depends exponentially on ℳλ\mathcal{M}_{\lambda}. When the bounded 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} ℳλ\mathcal{M}_{\lambda} scales at most logarithmically with the system size NN, polynomially many training samples suffice to learn all expectation-value functions in ℱ𝒰λ\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}_{\lambda}}. By contrast, when ℳλ\mathcal{M}_{\lambda} grows superlogarithmically, there exist circuit families in ℱ𝒰λ\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}_{\lambda}} whose expectation-value functions cannot be learned sample-efficiently by any classical learner. These results provide a resource-theoretic characterization of the classically learnable regime, revealing both the capabilities and the fundamental limitations of classical surrogates.

We then characterize the remaining part of the phase diagram by comparing classical learning with classical simulation. We relate 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} to operator stabilizer entropy (𝖮𝖲𝖤\mathsf{OSE}) [dowling2025magic], an instance-wise measure of quantum magic, and show that 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} is upper-bounded by 𝖮𝖲𝖤\mathsf{OSE} in the worst-case setting. This relation implies that the classically simulable regime is contained within the classically learnable regime. Moreover, we develop a 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided classical surrogate h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} that uses a quantum subroutine to identify dominant frequency modes and construct a compact predictive model. Our runtime analysis shows that h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} remains computationally efficient for learning ℱ𝒰λ\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}_{\lambda}} throughout the low-𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} regime, thereby turning the information-theoretic learnability guarantee into an implementable learning protocol. Under standard complexity-theoretic assumptions, we further show that classical algorithms without access to quantum-generated training data cannot attain comparable computational guarantees for simulating ℱ𝒰λ\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}_{\lambda}} in this regime. This establishes a rigorous computational separation between classical simulators and classical surrogates, demonstrating that learning can remain efficient beyond the reach of direct classical simulation. Together, these results complete the computational phase diagram in Fig. 1 and provide a resource-theoretic map for determining when description-only classical simulation or quantum-data-assisted emulation is preferable.

We conduct systematic numerical experiments to validate these theoretical findings up to 8080-qubit. The numerical results reproduce the theoretically predicted computational landscape in Fig. 1c, with 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} serving as a dividing line between classically learnable and non-learnable regimes, and 𝖮𝖲𝖤\mathsf{OSE} characterizing the boundary between classically simulable and learnable regimes.

II Main Result

II.1 Problem setup

We study mean-value estimation of an observable on states prepared by a family of parametrized quantum circuits. As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), for an observable O=∑l=1qOlO=\sum_{l=1}^{q}O_{l} with ∑l‖Ol‖∞≤1\sum_{l}\|O_{l}\|_{\infty}\leq 1, we consider the function class

ℱ𝒰={f⁡(𝒙)=Tr⁡(ρ0,O⁡(𝒙,U))|U∈𝒰},\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}}=\Big\{f(\bm{x})=\Tr\big(\rho_{0},O(\bm{x};U)\big)~\big|~U\in\mathcal{U}\Big\}, (1)

where ρ0\rho_{0} is an arbitrary NN-qubit state, 𝒙∈[−π,π]d\bm{x}\in[-\pi,\pi]^{d}, and O⁡(𝒙,U):=U​(𝒙)†​O​U​(𝒙)O(\bm{x};U):=U(\bm{x})^{\dagger}OU(\bm{x}) is the Heisenberg-evolved observable. Here, we focus on a restricted circuit family 𝒰⊂𝖠𝗋𝖼⁡(N,d)\mathcal{U}\subset\mathsf{Arc}(N,d), where the set 𝖠𝗋𝖼⁡(N,d)\mathsf{Arc}(N,d) collects all NN-qubit circuits U⁡(𝒙)=∏j=1d(RZ⁡(𝒙j)​Vj)U(\bm{x})=\prod_{j=1}^{d}(\RZ(\bm{x}_{j})V_{j}) of GG gates, comprising dd tunable rotation gates RZ\RZ interleaved with fixed blocks VjV_{j} from a universal gate set [nielsen2010quantum] (e.g., {H,S,T,CNOT}\{H,S,T,\CNOT\}), in an arbitrary layout. Each UU defines one mean-value function f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}), so ℱ𝒰\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}} collects these functions across all U∈𝒰U\in\mathcal{U}. Such estimation tasks underlie a broad range of applications, including digital quantum simulation [feynman2018simulating, zhang2022digital], quantum metrology [degen2017quantum, koczor2020variational], variational quantum algorithms [cerezo2021variational_VQA], and quantum-system certification [eisert2020quantum, Flammia201111dirct].

The objective of mean-value estimation in Eq. (1) is to use a classical model h⁡(𝒙)h(\bm{x}) to approximate f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}) for varying 𝒙\bm{x}. Following standard practice, the quality of h⁡(𝒙)h(\bm{x}) is measured by the average prediction error, or expected risk [gao2018efficient, huang2022provably, lerch2024efficient, fontana2025classical, du2025efficient, angrisani2025classically, liao2025demonstration], under an input distribution 𝔻\mathbb{D}, i.e.,

𝖱⁡(h)=𝔼𝒙∼𝔻​|h⁡(𝒙)−f⁡(𝒙)|2.\mathsf{R}(h)=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}\sim\mathbb{D}}\left|h(\bm{x})-f(\bm{x})\right|^{2}. (2)

This metric applies equally to classical simulators and to classical learning surrogates (see Supplementary Information (SI) A). The family ℱ𝒰\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}} is said to be classically efficient if, for any f∈ℱ𝒰f\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}} and a fixed target accuracy ϵ\epsilon, such an h⁡(𝒙)h(\bm{x}) can be constructed in time polynomial in the qubit count NN and the input dimension dd while achieving 𝖱⁡(h)≤ϵ\mathsf{R}(h)\leq\epsilon with high probability. When 𝔻\mathbb{D} is a point mass, ℱ𝒰\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}} collapses to a single circuit instance and is efficient for classical simulators when 𝒰\mathcal{U} consists of circuits containing low instance-wise quantum resources such as magic [bravyi2016improved, leone2022stabilizer] and entanglement [cirac2021matrix, markov2008simulating]. However, for a general 𝔻\mathbb{D}, which quantum resource governs the computational efficiency of ℱ𝒰\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}} for a restricted class 𝒰\mathcal{U} remains largely open, leaving the computational separation among classical simulators and classical surrogates unclear.

II.2 Dynamical stabilizer entropy

To address this question, we propose a new resource measure, dubbed dynamical stabilizer entropy (𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}). To define 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} formally, we first expand each target function f⁡(𝒙)∈ℱ𝒰f(\bm{x})\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}} for any 𝒰⊂𝖠𝗋𝖼⁡(N,d)\mathcal{U}\subset\mathsf{Arc}(N,d) in the trigonometric basis via its Pauli-transfer-matrix representation [greenbaum2015introduction], namely

f⁡(𝒙)=∑𝝎∈ΛΦ𝝎​(𝒙)​Tr⁡(ρ0​Q𝝎),f(\bm{x})=\sum_{\bm{\omega}\in\Lambda}\Phi_{\bm{\omega}}(\bm{x})\Tr(\rho_{0}Q_{\bm{\omega}}), (3)

where the trigonometric basis at the mode 𝝎\bm{\omega} is Φ𝝎​(𝒙)=∏j=1d[𝟙𝝎j=0+cos⁡(𝒙j),𝟙𝝎j=1+sin⁡(𝒙j),𝟙𝝎j=−1]\Phi_{\bm{\omega}}(\bm{x})=\prod_{j=1}^{d}[\mathbbm{1}_{\bm{\omega}_{j}=0}+\cos(\bm{x}_{j}),\mathbbm{1}_{\bm{\omega}_{j}=1}+\sin(\bm{x}_{j}),\mathbbm{1}_{\bm{\omega}_{j}=-1}], the operator Q𝝎Q_{\bm{\omega}} is a linear combination of Pauli strings, and Λ={−1,0,1}d\Lambda=\{-1,0,1\}^{d} is the frequency set with |Λ|=3d|\Lambda|=3^{d} [du2025efficient]. As illustrated in Fig. 1b, the number of modes that contribute to f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}), i.e., those 𝝎\bm{\omega} with Tr⁡(ρ0​Q𝝎)≠0\Tr(\rho_{0}Q_{\bm{\omega}})\neq 0, is governed by the circuit layout UU in 𝖠𝗋𝖼⁡(N,d)\mathsf{Arc}(N,d), and can grow exponentially with dd.

𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} essentially quantifies how broadly f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}) spreads over Λ\Lambda. In this measure, the fixed gates VjV_{j} in Eq. (1) are free operations, whereas the tunable rotations RZ⁡(𝒙j)\RZ(\bm{x}_{j}) are resource-generating. Formally, the α\alpha-order 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} is

ℳ(α)​[O⁡(𝒙,U)]=maxV∈𝕊​𝕌​(2N)⁡𝒮(α)​[V†​O​(𝒙,U)​V],\mathcal{M}^{(\alpha)}[O(\bm{x};U)]=\max_{V\in\mathbb{S}\mathbb{U}(2^{N})}\mathcal{S}^{(\alpha)}[V^{\dagger}O(\bm{x};U)V], (4)

where 𝒮(α)​[⋅]\mathcal{S}^{(\alpha)}[\cdot] is the order-α\alpha Rényi entropy of the mode distribution induced by the operator V†​O​(𝒙,U)​VV^{\dagger}O(\bm{x};U)V. Following Eq. (3), its expansion is ∑𝝎∈ΛΦ𝝎​(𝒙)​Q𝝎′\sum_{\bm{\omega}\in\Lambda}\Phi_{\bm{\omega}}(\bm{x})Q^{\prime}_{\bm{\omega}}. As a result, the induced distribution takes the form as p⁡(𝝎)=p~​(𝝎)/∑𝝎∈Λp~​(𝝎)\mathrm{p}(\bm{\omega})=\tilde{\mathrm{p}}(\bm{\omega})/\sum_{\bm{\omega}\in\Lambda}\tilde{\mathrm{p}}(\bm{\omega}) with p~​(𝝎)=𝔼𝒙∼𝔻​Φ𝝎​(𝒙)2​Tr⁡(ρ0​Q𝝎′)2\tilde{\mathrm{p}}(\bm{\omega})=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}\sim\mathbb{D}}\Phi_{\bm{\omega}}(\bm{x})^{2}\Tr(\rho_{0}Q^{\prime}_{\bm{\omega}})^{2}, recording the average squared contribution of each mode, and 𝒮(α)​[V†​O​(𝒙,U)​V]=(1−α)−1​log⁡(∑𝝎∈Λpα​(𝝎))\mathcal{S}^{(\alpha)}[V^{\dagger}O(\bm{x};U)V]=(1-\alpha)^{-1}\log\big(\sum_{\bm{\omega}\in\Lambda}\mathrm{p}^{\alpha}(\bm{\omega})\big). For brevity, we write ℳ(α)​[O​(𝒙,U)]\mathcal{M}^{(\alpha)}[O(\bm{x};U)] as shorthand, leaving the average over 𝔻\mathbb{D} and the maximization over VV implicit when they are clear from context.

The following theorem establishes that 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} is a valid quantum resource monotone [chitambar2019quantum] and bounds it against the operator stabilizer entropy (𝖮𝖲𝖤\mathsf{OSE}) [dowling2025magic], 𝔐ose(α)​[O⁡(𝒙,U)]\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{ose}}^{(\alpha)}[O(\bm{x};U)], an instance-wise magic monotone for the nonstabilizerness of O⁡(𝒙,U)O(\bm{x};U). The proofs are deferred to SI. B.

Theorem 1 (Informal).

Following Eqs. (1)-(4), 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} is non-negative and invariant under fixed gates. Given the class 𝖠𝗋𝖼⁡(N,d)\mathsf{Arc}(N,d), we have maxU∈𝖠𝗋𝖼⁡(N,d)⁡ℳ(α)​[O⁡(𝐱,U)]≲d\max_{U\in\mathsf{Arc}(N,d)}\mathcal{M}^{(\alpha)}[O(\bm{x};U)]\lesssim d, where the symbol ≲\lesssim hides constant factors. When d≤Nd\leq N, we have d≲max𝐱,U∈𝖠𝗋𝖼⁡(N,d)⁡𝔐ose(α)​[O⁡(𝐱,U)]d\lesssim\max_{\bm{x},U\in\mathsf{Arc}(N,d)}\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{ose}}^{(\alpha)}[O(\bm{x};U)].

These two inequalities determine the infeasible region of the computational phase diagram in Fig. 1c. For a fixed number of rotation gates dd, the worst-case 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} scales at most as 𝒪⁡(d)\mathcal{O}(d), whereas the worst-case 𝖮𝖲𝖤\mathsf{OSE} scales at least as Ω⁡(d)\Omega(d). In other words, all worst-case operating points lie on or below the diagonal 𝖣𝖲𝖤=𝖮𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}=\mathsf{OSE}, leading the upper-left triangle in Fig. 1c infeasible. The computational separation among classical simulators and classical surrogates therefore appears in the lower-right region.

Beyond its role as a monotone, 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} lifts the resource-theoretic characterization provided by 𝖮𝖲𝖤\mathsf{OSE} from a single instance to an entire parametrized circuit family ℱ𝒰\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}}. This lifting connects 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} to related resource measures, including state stabilizer Rényi entropy [leone2022stabilizer], unitary stabilizer nullity [jiang2023lower], and circuit complexity [bu2024complexity]. It also yields a family-level notion of compressibility. Low entanglement enables tensor-network truncation [cirac2021matrix], low 𝖮𝖲𝖤\mathsf{OSE} enables Pauli-path truncation [rudolph2023classical], and low 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} enables efficient construction of Pauli-path simulators and classical surrogates across ℱ𝒰\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}}. Similarly, dynamical properties studied through 𝖮𝖲𝖤\mathsf{OSE}, such as the growth, locality, and scrambling of operator magic [dowling2025magic], can be reformulated for ℱ𝒰\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}} as questions about how tunable circuits U⁡(𝒙)U(\bm{x}) generate and distribute operator magic across parameter space. In this sense, 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} provides a family-wide diagnostic of the classical accessibility of parametrized quantum dynamics. Further discussions are provided in SI. B.

II.3 Classical learnability of ℱ𝒰\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}} in terms of 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}

We now use 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} to delineate the classical learnability of ℱ𝒰λ\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}_{\lambda}} for the circuit family 𝒰λ\mathcal{U}_{\lambda} with bounded 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}. In particular, we consider the circuit family

𝒰λ={U∈𝖠𝗋𝖼⁡(N,d):ℳ(1)​[O⁡(𝒙,U)]≤ℳλ}\mathcal{U}_{\lambda}=\{U\in\mathsf{Arc}(N,d):\mathcal{M}^{(1)}[O(\bm{x};U)]\leq\mathcal{M}_{\lambda}\} (5)

Here, λ\lambda labels the circuit class, while ℳλ\mathcal{M}_{\lambda} denotes its 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} bound. The learnability of ℱ𝒰λ\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}_{\lambda}} follows by combining a sample-complexity characterization with an explicit runtime analysis. The former gives an information-theoretic criterion for sample-efficient learning, while the latter verifies that the same 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} threshold controls the cost of an implementable surrogate. Together, they identify where classical learning is both statistically and computationally efficient.

To set the stage, we briefly recall the classical learning protocols. Classical learners (or classical surrogates) are model-agnostic and receive the training set 𝒯={(𝒙(i),y(i))}i=1n\mathcal{T}=\{(\bm{x}^{(i)},y^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^{n}, where 𝒙(i)∼𝔻\bm{x}^{(i)}\sim\mathbb{D} on [−π,π]d[-\pi,\pi]^{d} and each label y(i)y^{(i)} is estimated from mm incoherent measurements. After training, a classical learner runs the trained predictor h⁡(𝒙)h(\bm{x}) on classical hardware at the inference stage without any access to a quantum device.

The lemma below characterizes the sample complexity of classical learning ℱ𝒰λ\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}_{\lambda}} in terms of the first-order 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}, with the formal statement and proof deferred to SI. C-E.

Lemma 1 (Informal).

Following Eqs. (1)-(5). Let νf=𝔼𝐱∼[−π,π]d​f​(𝐱)2\nu_{f}=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}\sim[-\pi,\pi]^{d}}f(\bm{x})^{2} and ϵ<νf/4\epsilon<\nu_{f}/4, and 𝒰λ⊂𝖠𝗋𝖼⁡(N,d)\mathcal{U}_{\lambda}\subset\mathsf{Arc}(N,d) be the circuit class with bounded 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}, i.e., ℳ(1)​[O⁡(𝐱,U)]≤ℳλ\mathcal{M}^{(1)}[O(\bm{x};U)]\leq\mathcal{M}_{\lambda} for any U∈𝒰λU\in\mathcal{U}_{\lambda}. Given 𝒯\mathcal{T}, the training data size

Ω⁡(2ℳλm​νf)≤n≤𝒪~​(212​νf​ℳλ/ϵ⋅dϵ)\Omega\Big(\frac{2^{\mathcal{M}_{\lambda}}}{m\nu_{f}}\Big)\leq n\leq\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\Big(\frac{2^{12\nu_{f}\mathcal{M}_{\lambda}/\epsilon}\cdot d}{\epsilon}\Big) (6)

is sufficient and necessary to achieve ϵ\epsilon-prediction error in Eq. (2) for a classical surrogate h⁡(𝐱)h(\bm{x}) with high probability. Here h⁡(𝐱)h(\bm{x}) has a model dimension 𝒪~​(212​νf​ℳλ/ϵ)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(2^{12\nu_{f}\mathcal{M}_{\lambda}/\epsilon}).

Lemma 1 captures the classically learnable regime of ℱ𝒰λ\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}_{\lambda}} for the circuit subset 𝒰λ⊂𝖠𝗋𝖼⁡(N,d)\mathcal{U}_{\lambda}\subset\mathsf{Arc}(N,d) along the horizontal boundary in Fig. 1c. The exponential dependence of both the upper and lower bounds in Eq. (6) on 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} establishes 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} as an exact dividing line for classical learnability. When ℳλ=maxU⁡ℳ(1)​[O⁡(𝒙,U)]=𝒪⁡(log⁡N)\mathcal{M}_{\lambda}=\max_{U}\mathcal{M}^{(1)}[O(\bm{x};U)]=\mathcal{O}(\log N), polynomially many samples and a polynomial-size model suffice for classical surrogates to reach 𝖱⁡(h)≤ϵ\mathsf{R}(h)\leq\epsilon. Beyond this regime, the sample complexity grows exponentially in NN. Together with ℳ(1)​[O⁡(𝒙,U)]≲d\mathcal{M}^{(1)}[O(\bm{x};U)]\lesssim d from Theorem 1, this criterion places all families ℱ𝒰\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}} with d=𝒪⁡(log⁡N)d=\mathcal{O}(\log N) tunable rotations on the classically learnable side and refines prior sample complexity bounds based on the number of tunable gates [leone2024learning, chia2024efficient, grewal2025efficient, bu2022statistical, bu2023effects, molteni2024exponential]. Thus, learnability is governed not by tunability alone, but by how broadly the target function spreads across frequency modes.

Remark. The assumption ϵ≤νf/4\epsilon\leq\nu_{f}/4 in Lemma 1 stems from the lower bound and ensures that the two bounds in Eq. (6) share the same dependence on νf\nu_{f}.

To establish the computational side of the separation, we next construct a 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} and analyze its runtime. Its implementation has three stages: dataset construction, model construction, and inference. The dataset construction and inference stages follow standard classical surrogates, with 𝒯\mathcal{T} obtained from circuit queries and h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} deployed on classical hardware. The main new ingredient is model construction, where a quantum subroutine identifies informative modes Λ𝗊⊂Λ\Lambda_{\mathsf{q}}\subset\Lambda in Eq. (3).

The quantum subroutine identifies modes in Λ𝗊\Lambda_{\mathsf{q}} with non-negligible contributions to the target function f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}). Here, we assume coherent access to the unknown circuit U⁡(𝒙)U(\bm{x}), U​(𝒙)†U(\bm{x})^{\dagger}, and coherent operation of the tunable rotation gate during circuit execution. We emphasize that these coherent operations are only required in the training stage and still leave the classical surrogate model agnostic, as the layout of the fixed gates in U⁡(𝒙)U(\bm{x}) remains unknown to the surrogate. As shown in Fig. 1c, given this access and a qq-sparse Pauli representation O=∑l=1q𝒂l​PlO=\sum_{l=1}^{q}\bm{a}_{l}P_{l}, the subroutine prepares the state |ψ𝗊⟩=∑𝝎∈Λ𝒔𝝎​p⁡(𝝎)​|𝝎⟩\ket{\psi_{\mathsf{q}}}=\sum_{\bm{\omega}\in\Lambda}\bm{s}_{\bm{\omega}}\sqrt{\mathrm{p}(\bm{\omega})}\ket{\bm{\omega}} with 𝒔𝝎\bm{s}_{\bm{\omega}} being a sign factor, using a (N+d+⌈log⁡q⌉)(N+d+\lceil\log q\rceil)-qubit circuit with Θ⁡(q​N+G)\Theta(qN+G) gates. Measuring this state samples modes according to p⁡(𝝎)\mathrm{p}(\bm{\omega}) in Eq. (4). Since p⁡(𝝎)\mathrm{p}(\bm{\omega}) depends on the structure-specific coefficient Tr⁡(ρ0​Q𝝎)\Tr(\rho_{0}Q_{\bm{\omega}}), the samples are biased toward modes that are relevant to f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}). Repeating this procedure independently mfm_{f} times yields the mode set Λ𝗊\Lambda_{\mathsf{q}} used by the surrogate (see SI. F for details). Once Λ𝗊\Lambda_{\mathsf{q}} is constructed, the surrogate predicts a new input 𝒙\bm{x} as

h𝗊​(𝒙)=1n​∑i=1nκ𝗊​(𝒙,𝒙(i))​y(i),h_{\mathsf{q}}(\bm{x})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\kappa_{\mathsf{q}}(\bm{x},\bm{x}^{(i)})y^{(i)}, (7)

where κ𝗊​(𝒙,𝒙(i))=∑𝝎∈Λ𝗊2‖𝝎‖0​Φ𝝎​(𝒙)​Φ𝝎​(𝒙(i))\kappa_{\mathsf{q}}(\bm{x},\bm{x}^{(i)})=\sum_{\bm{\omega}\in\Lambda_{\mathsf{q}}}2^{\|\bm{\omega}\|_{0}}\Phi_{\bm{\omega}}(\bm{x})\Phi_{\bm{\omega}}(\bm{x}^{(i)}) is the partial trigonometric-monomial kernel.

The resulting efficiency guarantee is stated below, with formal statement and proof deferred to SI. G.

Theorem 2 (Informal).

Following Eqs. (1)–(7), it suffices to use mf=𝒪~​(22​νf​ℳλ/ϵ​log⁡(2/δ))m_{f}=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(2^{2\nu_{f}\mathcal{M}_{\lambda}/\epsilon}\log(2/\delta)\right) independent frequency draws. The quantum subroutine then returns the set Λ𝗊\Lambda_{\mathsf{q}} of distinct observed modes, with d𝗊:=|Λ𝗊|≤mfd_{\mathsf{q}}:=|\Lambda_{\mathsf{q}}|\leq m_{f}, in expected time 𝒪⁡((q​N+G)​mf​‖𝐚‖1/νf)\mathcal{O}\left((qN+G)m_{f}\|\bm{a}\|_{1}/\sqrt{\nu_{f}}\right). A training-set size n=4​d𝗊/(ϵ​δ)n=4d_{\mathsf{q}}/(\epsilon\delta) then suffices to ensure 𝖱⁡(h𝗊)≤ϵ\mathsf{R}(h_{\mathsf{q}})\leq\epsilon with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta.

Theorem 2 and Lemma 1 together delineate the learnable regime for classical surrogates in Fig. 1c, where 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} acts as the efficiency threshold. For the circuit class 𝒰λ\mathcal{U}_{\lambda} with a low-𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} bound where ℳλ=𝒪⁡(log⁡N)\mathcal{M}_{\lambda}=\mathcal{O}(\log N), the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} has polynomial sample complexity and runtime. Once 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} grows beyond logarithmic size, the achieved sample-complexity lower bound in Lemma 1 and runtime scaling in Theorem 2 imply a cost exponential in ℳλ\mathcal{M}_{\lambda}, making classical learning of ℱ𝒰λ\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}_{\lambda}} intractable.

Remark. Details of the quantum subroutine are provided in Methods. For νf≤𝒪⁡(1/poly⁡(N))\nu_{f}\leq\mathcal{O}(1/\poly(N)), the classical learner can determine a trivial constant surrogate to achieve 𝖱⁡(h𝗊)≤ϵ\mathsf{R}(h_{\mathsf{q}})\leq\epsilon in polynomial runtime.

II.4 Separation between classical simulators and learners

We last compare classical surrogates with classical simulators. According to Eq. (3), efficient classical simulation always entails efficient learnability, since a simulator can generate training labels for a classical model (see SI. A.2 for details). The nontrivial question is whether the converse fails, namely whether some mean-value tasks are learnable from quantum-generated data but not simulable from their circuit descriptions alone.

The theorem below answers this question affirmatively, where the full statement and proof are deferred to SI. H.

Theorem 3 (Informal).

Consider a randomized classical algorithm 𝒞\mathcal{C} that does not learn from quantum-generated data. Suppose that, for any polynomial-depth circuit ensemble {U⁡(𝐱):𝐱∈[−π,π]d}\{U(\bm{x}):\bm{x}\in[-\pi,\pi]^{d}\} with ℳ(1)​[O⁡(𝐱,U)]≤𝒪⁡(log⁡N)\mathcal{M}^{(1)}[O(\bm{x};U)]\leq\mathcal{O}(\log N), 𝒞\mathcal{C} outputs an efficiently evaluable hypothesis f^\hat{f} satisfying 𝖱⁡(f^)≤ϵ\mathsf{R}(\hat{f})\leq\epsilon. Then arbitrary 𝖡𝖰𝖯\mathsf{BQP} computations can be simulated by a randomized polynomial-time classical algorithm, i.e., 𝖡𝖰𝖯⊆𝖡𝖯𝖯\mathsf{BQP}\subseteq\mathsf{BPP}.

Theorem 3 reveals that matching the low-𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} surrogate without quantum-generated data would collapse standard quantum and classical complexity classes. The achieved result completes the phase diagram in Fig. 1c, i.e., in the low-𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} regime, classical learners can outperform description-only classical simulators. Consequently, circuit families ℱ𝒰\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{U}} may still be learnable even when their individual instances are highly entangled and magic-rich, placing them beyond the reach of classical simulators, e.g., tensor-network simulators [cirac2021matrix] and near-Clifford or Pauli-propagation methods [bravyi2016improved, leone2022stabilizer]. This separates learnability from simulability and provides a resource-theoretic perspective on quantum learning theory, complementing prior approaches based on quantum data, classical shadows, and surrogate models [huang2022quantum, schreiber2023classical, jerbi2023shadows].

The proposed 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}}, together with Theorem 3, gives a practical criterion for when a classical surrogate suffices after training. At low 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}, finite quantum measurements can be converted into a reusable classical surrogate, enabling predictions at new settings even when individual instances remain beyond description-only simulation. This replaces repeated quantum queries with a one-time training cost in tasks that evaluate a parametrized family many times, such as digital quantum simulation across Hamiltonian parameters and evolution times [feynman2018simulating, zhang2022digital, kim2023evidence], variational quantum algorithms [cerezo2021variational_VQA, peruzzo2014variational], and quantum certification routines [eisert2020quantum, Flammia201111dirct]. In this regard, the achieved separation clarifies a form of quantum-data-assisted utility, where the processor generates hard-to-simulate training data, and the classical surrogate handles subsequent predictions.

III Numerical results

We conduct numerical simulations on quantum circuits with up to 8080 qubits to assess the efficiency of the proposed 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided classical surrogate h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} and its separation in prediction performance from conventional classical surrogates and classical simulators, as established theoretically and illustrated in Fig. 1c. Implementation details and additional numerical results, including applications of 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided classical surrogates to the classical optimization of variational quantum algorithms (VQAs), are provided in SI. I.

We first evaluate the prediction performance of h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} on random quantum circuits UrU_{\mathrm{r}} with a fixed system size N=6N=6 and circuit depth L=66L=66, while varying 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}. Each circuit contains a prescribed number GTG_{T} of TT gates and CNOT gates inserted with probability γ\gamma, with a random gate layout. Unless otherwise stated, we set GT=6G_{T}=6 and γ=0.1\gamma=0.1. The observable is fixed as O=Z1⋯ZNO=Z_{1}\cdots Z_{N}. We vary the number of tunable rotation gates as d∈{2,4,6,8}d\in\{2,4,6,8\}, thereby generating circuits with different values of 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}. To construct h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}}, we consider four different feature dimensions, D:=|Λ𝗊|∈{1,2,4,8},D:=|\Lambda_{\mathsf{q}}|\in\{1,2,4,8\}, where DD also controls the computational cost of classical inference. For all methods, prediction performance is quantified by the coefficient of determination R2R^{2}, evaluated on a test set of 200200 samples.

Fig. 2a compares the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} with the Hamming-weight surrogate h𝖼h_{\mathsf{c}} of Refs. [du2025efficient, liao2025demonstration] for varying training-set size n∈{2,5,10,20,60}n\in\{2,5,10,20,60\} and D∈{1,2,4,8}D\in\{1,2,4,8\}. For both settings of d={2,8}d=\{2,8\}, increasing the feature dimension dd and nn could constantly improve the prediction accuracy of h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}}. In particular, when d=2d=2, h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} constructed with d=1d=1 and n=10n=10 suffices to achieve the perfect prediction with R2≈1R^{2}\approx 1, whereas h𝖼h_{\mathsf{c}} requires (D,n)=(8,20)(D,n)=(8,20) to reach a comparable accuracy. The difference becomes sharper at d=6d=6. With only D=2D=2 features, h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} reaches R2=0.96R^{2}=0.96 at n=5n=5, while h𝖼h_{\mathsf{c}} remains at R2=0R^{2}=0 throughout the displayed range.

We next directly test the operational role of 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}. Fig. 2b collects the results for varying d∈{2,4,6,8}d\in\{2,4,6,8\} and D∈{1,2,4,8}D\in\{1,2,4,8\} at fixed n=20n=20. Here, we employ 𝒮(1)\mathcal{S}^{(1)} as a tractable proxy of 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}. Across the resulting 1616 configurations, the prediction accuracy is strongly anticorrelated with this entropy, with Pearson coefficient r=−0.916r=-0.916 and p=6.4×10−7p=6.4\times 10^{-7}. In particular, the low-entropy instances attain R2≈1R^{2}\approx 1, whereas the largest observed entropy, 𝒮(1)≈3\mathcal{S}^{(1)}\approx 3, reduces the accuracy to R2=0.38R^{2}=0.38 even when more features are retained. These results accord with Theorem 2 and highlight that the relevant features identified by the quantum subroutine provide a substantially more compact representation than a truncation based only on Hamming weight.

To compare the inference efficiency of learning with conventional simulation, we first vary the rate of inserting CNOT gates γ∈{0.01,0.02,0.04,0.08,0.1}\gamma\in\{0.01,0.02,0.04,0.08,0.1\} while fixing d=6d=6 and n=100n=100. Fig. 2c reports averaged prediction performance of h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} with D={2,4}D=\{2,4\} and a matrix-product-state (MPS) simulator at matched truncation parameters χ={2,4}\chi=\{2,4\} to ensure the inference cost of h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} less than the cost of MPS. At DD(χ\chi)=4=4, the MPS accuracy rapidly decreases from R2=1R^{2}=1 for γ≤0.02\gamma\leq 0.02 to 00 at 0.10.1, respectively. In contrast, h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} maintains R2≥0.92R^{2}\geq 0.92 over the same range. The same qualitative separation is visible at DD(χ\chi)=2=2, where h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} retains R2≥0.75R^{2}\geq 0.75 while the MPS result approaches zero. These results highlight the prediction advantage of h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} over the tensor-network simulation methods for highly entangled quantum circuits.

Fig. 2d extends this comparison to structured quantum circuits of size N=31N=31 with varied 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} and 𝖮𝖲𝖤\mathsf{OSE}. To this end, we consider the quantum circuit of form U⁡(𝒙)=∏j=1dRZj⁡(𝒙j)​∏j=d+1d+GtTk​∏j=2d+GtCNOT1,j⁡H1U(\bm{x})=\prod_{j=1}^{d}\RZ_{j}(\bm{x}_{j})\prod_{j=d+1}^{d+G_{t}}T_{k}\prod_{j=2}^{d+G_{t}}\CNOT_{1,j}H_{1} with the observable O=X1⋯Xd+GtO=X_{1}\cdots X_{d+G_{t}}, which allows us to vary the worst-case 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} and 𝖮𝖲𝖤\mathsf{OSE} by varying dd and GtG_{t}. The left panel evaluates the relation between 𝖮𝖲𝖤\mathsf{OSE} and 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} and shows that all displayed instances lie in the allowed region 𝖣𝖲𝖤≤𝖮𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}\leq\mathsf{OSE}, in agreement with Theorem 1. The remaining panels compare a Pauli-path simulator (PPS), h𝖼h_{\mathsf{c}}, and h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} using n=400n=400 and a common truncation budget D=16D=16. PPS is accurate mainly when the 𝖮𝖲𝖤\mathsf{OSE}-related quantity Gt+dG_{t}+d is small, whereas h𝖼h_{\mathsf{c}} is largely confined to the lowest-𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} edge. By contrast, h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} retains a substantially broader high-accuracy region, including circuits with a large 𝖮𝖲𝖤\mathsf{OSE}. These results indicate the computational boundary of classical simulators (as highlighted by the vertical line at Gt+d=5G_{t}+d=5) and classical surrogates (as highlighted by the horizontal line at ℳ(1)=5\mathcal{M}^{(1)}=5), therefore providing a numerical counterpart of the established separation depicted in Fig. 1c.

Finally, we examine the scalability behavior of h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} at large scale. Specifically, we consider the quantum circuit U⁡(𝒙)=∏i=1N−1CZi,i+1​∏i=1dTi​RZi⁡(xi)​∏i=1NHiU(\bm{x})=\prod_{i=1}^{N-1}\mathrm{CZ}_{i,i+1}\prod_{i=1}^{d}T_{i}\RZ_{i}(x_{i})\prod_{i=1}^{N}H_{i} with the observable O=1d−k+1​∑i=1d−k+1∏j=ii+k−1OjO=\frac{1}{d-k+1}\sum_{i=1}^{d-k+1}\prod_{j=i}^{i+k-1}O_{j}, where Oj=Zj−1​Xj​Zj+1O_{j}=Z_{j-1}X_{j}Z_{j+1} and k=5k=5. We consider six combinations of qubit size and the number of rotation gates, (N,d)={(20,6),(30,9),(40,12),(50,15),(60,18),(80,21)}(N,d)=\{(20,6),(30,9),(40,12),(50,15),(60,18),(80,21)\}. As shown in Fig. 3b, the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} proxy 𝒮(1)\mathcal{S}^{(1)} grows from approximately 66 to 99 across these instances. Fig. 3a shows the prediction performance of h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} and h𝖼h_{\mathsf{c}} with varying feature dimension and training set size (D,n)={(50,100),(100,200),(200,300),(300,500),(700,700)}(D,n)=\{(50,100),(100,200),(200,300),(300,500),(700,700)\}. As the system size NN grows from 2020 to 8080, the required training examples for h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} to achieve R2≈1R^{2}\approx 1 increase from 200200 to 700700. Importantly, this moderate increase in sample complexity accompanies the growth of 𝒮(1)\mathcal{S}^{(1)}. These results highlight that the prediction performance of h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} is governed primarily by 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} rather than directly by the system size, thereby demonstrating its scalability.

IV Discussions

We have characterized the classical learnability of quantum circuits from a resource-theoretic standpoint. Introducing the dynamical stabilizer entropy (𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}) as a resource measure, we proved that 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} governs both the sample and computational efficiency of classical surrogates, and we built an explicit 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate that meets these guarantees. The diagonal boundary follows from Theorem 1 and marks the infeasible region where the worst-case 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} would exceed the corresponding instance-wise magic. The horizontal boundary, established by Lemma 1 and Theorem 2, separates low-𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} families that are learnable from quantum-generated data from high-𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} families where classical learning becomes intractable. Theorem 3 then distinguishes the lower-right region from purely classical simulation.

We further showed that the efficiently learnable regime can extend beyond classical simulability. Together, these results map out a resource-theoretic landscape linking classical surrogates and conventional simulators, sharpening the distinction between classical learnability and simulability and guiding the use of classical methods [Sweke2025potential, schreiber2023classical, du2025efficient, du2025artificial, liao2025demonstration, rudolph2026pauli, shao2026characterizing] to predict quantum-circuit behavior.

By bridging the classical learnability of quantum circuits with quantum resource theory, our work opens several directions. From a physics perspective, 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} provides a parameter-space diagnostic of operator spreading that complements real-space measures of scrambling, such as out-of-time-order correlators [nahum2018operator, leone2022stabilizer]. Establishing its connections to these dynamical quantities, as well as to the magic and entanglement generated during circuit evolution [nahum2017entanglement, bejan2024dynamical, niroula2024phase, turkeshi2025magic], could lead to a unified resource-theoretic picture of when quantum dynamics is learnable, simulable, or neither.

Another important direction is to determine how noise reshapes 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} and the performance of 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogates. Characterizing how realistic noise redistributes or suppresses the frequency modes of circuit expectation functions, and how these changes propagate into learning guarantees, would extend our framework to noisy quantum devices and inform the design of robust surrogates. Moving beyond the present independent-input setting is equally important. Correlated parameters and general input distributions, as encountered in Hamiltonian simulation [feynman2018simulating, zhang2022digital, kim2023evidence] and geometric quantum machine learning [ragone2022representation, perrier2024quantum, wiersema2025geometric], call for distribution-aware resource measures based on appropriate Fourier expansions of circuit expectation functions [schuld2021effect], together with efficient procedures for extracting the relevant Fourier coefficients [barthe2025quantum] and constructing the corresponding surrogates.

Finally, extending the resource-theoretic analysis to deep-learning-based surrogates [zhu2022flexible, wu2024variational, du2025artificial] could reveal whether analogous resources govern the learnability of nonlinear model classes. Progress along these directions would deepen the connection between quantum resource theory and classical learnability and broaden the applicability of classical surrogates for predicting quantum-circuit behaviour.
