G.3 Proof of Lemma 14

Proof of Lemma 14.

The proof uses Markov’s inequality, Pr⁡(X≥a)≤𝔼⁡[X]/a\Pr(X\geq a)\leq\mathbb{E}[X]/a, which holds for any non-negative random variable XX and a>0a>0. First, let X:=−log⁡(p⁡(𝝎))X:=-\log(\mathrm{p}(\bm{\omega})), where 𝝎∈{0,1,−1}d\bm{\omega}\in\{0,1,-1\}^{d} follows the distribution p⁡(𝝎)\mathrm{p}(\bm{\omega}). Then we have

𝔼⁡[X]=∑𝝎p⁡(𝝎)​log⁡(1p⁡(𝝎))=𝒮(1)​[O⁡(𝒙,U)].\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{\bm{\omega}}\mathrm{p}(\bm{\omega})\log\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{p}(\bm{\omega})}\right)=\mathcal{S}^{(1)}[O(\bm{x};U)]. (203)

Hence, using Markov’s inequality, we find that for any a>0a>0,

Pr𝝎∼p⁡(−log⁡(p⁡(𝝎))≥a)≤𝒮(1)​[O​(𝒙,U)]a⇔Pr𝝎∼p⁡(p⁡(𝝎)≤2−a)≤𝒮(1)​[O​(𝒙,U)]a,\Pr_{\bm{\omega}\sim p}(-\log(\mathrm{p}(\bm{\omega}))\geq a)\leq\frac{\mathcal{S}^{(1)}[O(\bm{x};U)]}{a}~~\Leftrightarrow~~\Pr_{\bm{\omega}\sim p}(\mathrm{p}(\bm{\omega})\leq 2^{-a})\leq\frac{\mathcal{S}^{(1)}[O(\bm{x};U)]}{a}, (204)

or equivalently, letting τ=2−a\tau=2^{-a},

∑𝝎∈Λ\Λτp⁡(𝝎)=Pr𝝎∼p⁡(p⁡(𝝎)≤τ)≤𝒮(1)​[O​(𝒙,U)]log⁡(1/τ)≤ℳ(1)​[O​(𝒙,U)]log⁡(1/τ),\sum_{\bm{\omega}\in\Lambda\backslash\Lambda_{\tau}}\mathrm{p}(\bm{\omega})=\Pr_{\bm{\omega}\sim p}(\mathrm{p}(\bm{\omega})\leq\tau)\leq\frac{\mathcal{S}^{(1)}[O(\bm{x};U)]}{\log(1/\tau)}\leq\frac{\mathcal{M}^{(1)}[O(\bm{x};U)]}{\log(1/\tau)}, (205)

where the second inequality follows the definition of ℳ(1)​[O​(𝒙,U)]\mathcal{M}^{(1)}[O(\bm{x};U)]. ∎

SI H Computational hardness for purely classical algorithms to emulate observable expectations

In this section, we complement the efficient surrogate-emulation result with a complexity-theoretic limitation for purely classical algorithms. Recall that the learnability guarantee established in Theorem 2 applies to a classical predictor trained with quantum-generated data. By contrast, a purely classical simulator receives only the classical description of the circuit and the observable, and has no access to measurement data from the quantum device. We prove that, under the standard complexity-theoretic conjecture 𝖡𝖰𝖯⊈𝖡𝖯𝖯\mathsf{BQP}\not\subseteq\mathsf{BPP}, there exists a circuit family that is efficiently learnable by the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate, yet cannot be emulated in polynomial time by any purely classical algorithm. In particular, for a fixed sufficiently small constant target error ϵ>0\epsilon>0, we will construct NN-qubit quantum circuits Uℓ​(𝒙)U_{\ell}(\bm{x}) containing d=𝒪⁡(min⁡{1/ϵ,N})d=\mathcal{O}(\min\{1/\epsilon,N\}) tunable rotation gates, which nevertheless yield a logarithmically scaling 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} for a specific observable OO, namely ℳ(1)​[O⁡(𝒙,Uℓ)]=𝒪⁡(log⁡N)\mathcal{M}^{(1)}[O(\bm{x};U_{\ell})]=\mathcal{O}(\log N).

The organization of this section is as follows. In SI. H.1, we present the explicit construction of the circuit family and establish the separation, i.e., the constructed family is efficiently learnable by the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate but is intractable for any purely classical algorithm unless 𝖡𝖰𝖯⊆𝖡𝖯𝖯\mathsf{BQP}\subseteq\mathsf{BPP}. In SI. H.2, we present the proofs of the two technical lemmas used in the above analysis.

H.1 Construction of the circuit family and the separation

The construction of the quantum circuits is based on the computational hardness of the 𝖡𝖰𝖯\mathsf{BQP} complexity class, whose hardness is embedded into the parameter-independent blocks of the circuit, while the tunable rotation gates are arranged to generate a low-𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} trigonometric structure. In this regard, we first recall the 𝖡𝖰𝖯\mathsf{BQP} complexity class.

𝖡𝖰𝖯\mathsf{BQP} complexity class. 𝖡𝖰𝖯\mathsf{BQP} (short for bounded-error quantum polynomial time) is the complexity class of promise problems that can be solved by polynomial-time quantum computations with a small probability of error [watrous2008quantum]. Concretely, for a language L∈𝖡𝖰𝖯L\in\mathsf{BQP} and an input ℓ\ell, there exists a uniform family of polynomial-size quantum circuits {Wℓ}\{W_{\ell}\} acting on m=m⁡(ℓ)=poly⁡(|ℓ|)m=m(\ell)=\mathrm{poly}(|\ell|) qubits initialized in |0m⟩\ket{0^{m}}, such that measuring the first output qubit in the computational basis yields an acceptance probability pℓp_{\ell} satisfying pℓ≥2/3p_{\ell}\geq 2/3 if ℓ∈L\ell\in L and pℓ≤1/3p_{\ell}\leq 1/3 if ℓ∉L\ell\notin L. It is widely believed that 𝖡𝖰𝖯⊈𝖡𝖯𝖯\mathsf{BQP}\not\subseteq\mathsf{BPP}; otherwise, problems such as integer factoring would admit randomized polynomial-time classical algorithms.

Explicit construction. Fix a language L∈𝖡𝖰𝖯L\in\mathsf{BQP}. For an arbitrary input ℓ\ell, standard error amplification yields a polynomial-size circuit WℓW_{\ell} on m=poly⁡(|ℓ|)m=\mathrm{poly}(|\ell|) qubits, compiled over the universal gate set {H,S,CNOT,T}\{H,S,\CNOT,T\}, whose first output qubit obeys

μℓ:=⟨0m|​Wℓ†​Z1​Wℓ​|0m⟩=1−2​pℓ,ℓ∈L⇒μℓ≤−13,ℓ∉L⇒μℓ≥13.\mu_{\ell}:=\bra{0^{m}}W_{\ell}^{\dagger}Z_{1}W_{\ell}\ket{0^{m}}=1-2p_{\ell},\qquad\ell\in L\Rightarrow\mu_{\ell}\leq-\tfrac{1}{3},\quad\ell\notin L\Rightarrow\mu_{\ell}\geq\tfrac{1}{3}. (206)

In other words, deciding the sign of μℓ\mu_{\ell} is equivalent to deciding the membership of ℓ\ell in LL. Let N=m+dN=m+d, where the dd additional qubits, indexed by m+1,…,m+dm+1,\dots,m+d, serve as probe qubits. We then define the NN-qubit circuit family

𝒰L={Uℓ(𝒙)=Wℓ⊗∏j=1dRZm+j(𝒙j)Hm+j|ℓ∈{0,1}∗,𝒙∈[−π,π]d},\mathcal{U}_{L}=\left\{U_{\ell}(\bm{x})=W_{\ell}\otimes\prod_{j=1}^{d}\RZ_{m+j}(\bm{x}_{j})\,H_{m+j}~\Big|~\ell\in\{0,1\}^{*},~\bm{x}\in[-\pi,\pi]^{d}\right\}, (207)

together with the fixed initial state ρ0=|0⟩​⟨0|⊗N\rho_{0}=\ket{0}\bra{0}^{\otimes N} and the fixed observable

O=1d​∑j=1dZ1​Xm+j,∑l‖Ol‖∞=1.O=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}Z_{1}\,X_{m+j},\qquad\sum_{l}\|O_{l}\|_{\infty}=1. (208)

Each Uℓ​(𝒙)U_{\ell}(\bm{x}) is an instance of the RZ+CI+T\RZ+\CI+T circuit of Eq. (1) with dd tunable rotations, where the parameter-independent gates, namely WℓW_{\ell} and the Hadamards, form the fixed blocks. In this way, the entire 𝖡𝖰𝖯\mathsf{BQP} hardness is placed into the fixed block WℓW_{\ell}, whereas the dd tunable probes generate the trigonometric structure of the target function. We emphasize that both ρ0\rho_{0} and OO are prescribed and independent of ℓ\ell, so that the unknown instance is carried solely by the circuit.

The following lemma shows that the mean-value function of the constructed family admits a product form, and that the resulting 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} for the evolved observable O⁡(𝒙,Uℓ)=Uℓ​(𝒙)†​O​Uℓ​(𝒙)O(\bm{x};U_{\ell})=U_{\ell}(\bm{x})^{\dagger}OU_{\ell}(\bm{x}) remains logarithmic in NN.

Lemma 15 (Product form and 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} bound).

For the circuit family 𝒰L\mathcal{U}_{L} and the observable OO defined in Eqs. (206)–(208), the mean-value function yields

fℓ​(𝒙)=Tr⁡(ρ0​Uℓ​(𝒙)†​O​Uℓ​(𝒙))=μℓ​h​(𝒙),withh⁡(𝒙)=1d​∑j=1dcos⁡(𝒙j).f_{\ell}(\bm{x})=\Tr\big(\rho_{0}\,U_{\ell}(\bm{x})^{\dagger}O\,U_{\ell}(\bm{x})\big)=\mu_{\ell}\,h(\bm{x}),\quad\text{with}\quad h(\bm{x})=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\cos(\bm{x}_{j}). (209)

Consequently, we have νf=𝔼𝐱​fℓ​(𝐱)2=μℓ2/(2​d)\nu_{f}=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}}f_{\ell}(\bm{x})^{2}=\mu_{\ell}^{2}/(2d) and ℳ(1)​[O⁡(𝐱,Uℓ)]≤log⁡(2​d)=𝒪⁡(log⁡N)\mathcal{M}^{(1)}[O(\bm{x};U_{\ell})]\leq\log(2d)=\mathcal{O}(\log N).

Building on the product form fℓ​(𝒙)=μℓ​h​(𝒙)f_{\ell}(\bm{x})=\mu_{\ell}h(\bm{x}), the next lemma provides a reduction showing that any accurate hypothesis f^\hat{f} of the target function fℓf_{\ell} can be converted into a decision procedure for the sign of μℓ\mu_{\ell}. The intuition is that, since the 𝒙\bm{x}-dependence of fℓf_{\ell} is entirely carried by the known function h⁡(𝒙)h(\bm{x}), correlating a hypothesis f^\hat{f} against hh isolates the unknown constant μℓ\mu_{\ell}.

Lemma 16 (Reduction to the decision problem of μℓ\mu_{\ell}).

Let f^\hat{f} satisfy 𝔼𝐱​|f^​(𝐱)−fℓ​(𝐱)|2≤ϵ\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}}|\hat{f}(\bm{x})-f_{\ell}(\bm{x})|^{2}\leq\epsilon with ϵ≤νf/16\epsilon\leq\nu_{f}/16. Then the estimator

μ^:=2​d​𝔼𝒙​[f^​(𝒙)​h​(𝒙)]obeys|μ^−μℓ|≤14​|μℓ|,\hat{\mu}:=2d\,\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}}\big[\hat{f}(\bm{x})\,h(\bm{x})\big]\quad\text{obeys}\quad|\hat{\mu}-\mu_{\ell}|\leq\tfrac{1}{4}|\mu_{\ell}|, (210)

so that sign⁡(μ^)=sign⁡(μℓ)\mathrm{sign}(\hat{\mu})=\mathrm{sign}(\mu_{\ell}) decides whether ℓ∈L\ell\in L. Moreover, μ^\hat{\mu} can be computed to accuracy 18​|μℓ|\tfrac{1}{8}|\mu_{\ell}| from M=𝒪⁡(d2​log⁡(1/δ))M=\mathcal{O}(d^{2}\log(1/\delta)) evaluations of f^\hat{f} and hh, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta.

Supported by Lemmas 15 and 16, whose proofs are deferred to SI. H.2, we are now ready to present the formal statement of the separation, in which the constructed family is simultaneously efficiently learnable by the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate and hard for any purely classical algorithm.

Theorem (Formal statement of Theorem 3).

Let L∈𝖡𝖰𝖯L\in\mathsf{BQP} be an arbitrary language and fix a universal constant 0<ϵ≤1/2880<\epsilon\leq 1/288. Consider the NN-qubit circuit family 𝒰L\mathcal{U}_{L} in Eq. (207) with d≥1d\geq 1 satisfying d​ϵ≤1/288d\epsilon\leq 1/288, the fixed initial state ρ0\rho_{0}, and the fixed observable OO in Eq. (208). The induced target function class is

ℱL={fℓ(𝒙)=Tr(ρ0Uℓ(𝒙)†OUℓ(𝒙))=μℓh(𝒙)|ℓ∈{0,1}∗,𝒙∈[−π,π]d}.\mathcal{F}_{L}=\left\{f_{\ell}(\bm{x})=\Tr\big(\rho_{0}\,U_{\ell}(\bm{x})^{\dagger}O\,U_{\ell}(\bm{x})\big)=\mu_{\ell}\,h(\bm{x})~\Big|~\ell\in\{0,1\}^{*},~\bm{x}\in[-\pi,\pi]^{d}\right\}. (211)

Then ℱL\mathcal{F}_{L} satisfies the following two properties.

  • (i)

    (Classically learnable.) For every input ℓ\ell, the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} achieves 𝔼𝒙​|h𝗊​(𝒙)−fℓ​(𝒙)|2≤ϵ\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}}|h_{\mathsf{q}}(\bm{x})-f_{\ell}(\bm{x})|^{2}\leq\epsilon using a feature dimension d𝗊≤mf=poly⁡(N)d_{\mathsf{q}}\leq m_{f}=\mathrm{poly}(N) and n=poly⁡(N)n=\mathrm{poly}(N) quantum-labeled samples.

  • (ii)

    (Classically non-simulable.) Suppose there exists a randomized polynomial-time classical algorithm which, without access to quantum-generated data, outputs for every input ℓ\ell a hypothesis f^\hat{f} satisfying 𝔼𝒙​|f^​(𝒙)−fℓ​(𝒙)|2≤ϵ\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}}|\hat{f}(\bm{x})-f_{\ell}(\bm{x})|^{2}\leq\epsilon. Then 𝖡𝖰𝖯⊆𝖡𝖯𝖯\mathsf{BQP}\subseteq\mathsf{BPP}.

Remark. The quantifier in property (ii) is over all inputs ℓ\ell rather than a single one, since deciding the membership ℓ∈L\ell\in L requires the classical algorithm to succeed on both the yes-instances and the no-instances of the promise problem. Accordingly, the index set of 𝒰L\mathcal{U}_{L} and ℱL\mathcal{F}_{L} ranges over all bit strings ℓ∈{0,1}∗\ell\in\{0,1\}^{*}, and the language LL enters only through the sign of μℓ\mu_{\ell} in Eq. (206).

Proof of Theorem 3.

This proof is composed of two parts, which separately establish the classical learnability and the classical hardness of the constructed family.

Classical learnability. This part follows by directly invoking Theorem 2, whose hypotheses are all met by the constructed target function class ℱL\mathcal{F}_{L}. Specifically, the initial state is the fixed product state ρ0=|0⟩​⟨0|⊗N\rho_{0}=\ket{0}\bra{0}^{\otimes N}, the circuit Uℓ​(𝒙)U_{\ell}(\bm{x}) has polynomial depth, and the observable OO is a sum of weight-two Pauli operators admitting direct eigenvalue measurement. Supported by Lemma 15, we have ℳ(1)​[O⁡(𝒙,Uℓ)]≤log⁡(2​d)\mathcal{M}^{(1)}[O(\bm{x};U_{\ell})]\leq\log(2d). Since |μℓ|≥1/3|\mu_{\ell}|\geq 1/3 and d​ϵ≤1/288d\epsilon\leq 1/288, we have

ϵ≤1288​d≤μℓ232​d=νf16.\epsilon\leq\frac{1}{288d}\leq\frac{\mu_{\ell}^{2}}{32d}=\frac{\nu_{f}}{16}. (212)

For the observable in Eq. (208), we have q=d,𝒂j=1/dq=d,\bm{a}_{j}=1/d, and hence ‖𝒂‖1=∑j=1d|𝒂j|=1\|\bm{a}\|_{1}=\sum_{j=1}^{d}|\bm{a}_{j}|=1. Moreover, we have

‖𝒂‖12νf=2​dμℓ2≤18​d=𝒪⁡(1/ϵ)=𝒪⁡(poly⁡(N)),\frac{\|\bm{a}\|_{1}^{2}}{\nu_{f}}=\frac{2d}{\mu_{\ell}^{2}}\leq 18d=\mathcal{O}(1/\epsilon)=\mathcal{O}(\poly(N)), (213)

where the inequality uses |μℓ|≥1/3|\mu_{\ell}|\geq 1/3 and the scaling follows from d​ϵ≤1/288d\epsilon\leq 1/288. Moreover, both ϵ\epsilon and d=𝒪⁡(1/ϵ)d=\mathcal{O}(1/\epsilon) are fixed independently of NN. Hence, at the target accuracy ϵ\epsilon, the exponent governing the model dimension obeys

2​νf​ℳ(1)​[O⁡(𝒙,Uℓ)]ϵ≤log⁡(2​d)d​μℓ2=𝒪⁡(1).\frac{2\nu_{f}\mathcal{M}^{(1)}[O(\bm{x};U_{\ell})]}{\epsilon}\leq\frac{\log(2d)}{d\mu_{\ell}^{2}}=\mathcal{O}(1). (214)

Consequently, the draw budget satisfies mf=𝒪~​(2OPEN2​νf​ℳ(1)​[O⁡(𝒙,Uℓ)])/ϵ)=poly⁡(N)m_{f}=\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(2^{2\nu_{f}\mathcal{M}^{(1)}[O(\bm{x};U_{\ell})])/\epsilon})=\poly(N) for the inverse-polynomial error ϵ\epsilon. Since d𝗊≤mfd_{\mathsf{q}}\leq m_{f}, the feature dimension is also polynomial in NN. Moreover, choosing n=4​d𝗊/(ϵ​δ)n=4d_{\mathsf{q}}/(\epsilon\delta) gives n=poly⁡(N,1/δ)n=\poly(N,1/\delta). Taken together, the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} emulates this family with polynomial sample complexity and runtime.

Hardness for purely classical algorithms. Suppose, for the sake of the argument, that a randomized polynomial-time classical algorithm without access to quantum-generated data outputs, for every input ℓ\ell, a hypothesis f^\hat{f} satisfying 𝔼𝒙​|f^​(𝒙)−fℓ​(𝒙)|2≤ϵ\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}}|\hat{f}(\bm{x})-f_{\ell}(\bm{x})|^{2}\leq\epsilon. As shown above, d​ϵ≤1/288d\epsilon\leq 1/288 and |μℓ|≥1/3|\mu_{\ell}|\geq 1/3 imply ϵ≤νf/16\epsilon\leq\nu_{f}/16. Employing Lemma 16, the estimator μ^\hat{\mu} can be computed from f^\hat{f} in randomized polynomial time and obeys sign⁡(μ^)=sign⁡(μℓ)\mathrm{sign}(\hat{\mu})=\mathrm{sign}(\mu_{\ell}). By Eq. (206), the sign of μℓ\mu_{\ell} decides whether ℓ∈L\ell\in L, so the above procedure decides the language LL in randomized polynomial time. Since L∈𝖡𝖰𝖯L\in\mathsf{BQP} was arbitrary, this yields a randomized polynomial-time classical decision procedure for every language in 𝖡𝖰𝖯\mathsf{BQP}, and hence 𝖡𝖰𝖯⊆𝖡𝖯𝖯\mathsf{BQP}\subseteq\mathsf{BPP}. This completes the proof. ∎

H.2 Proof of Lemmas 15 and 16

Here we present the proofs of the two technical lemmas used in the separation.

Proof of Lemma 15.

This proof consists of two parts, which separately derive the product form of fℓ​(𝒙)f_{\ell}(\bm{x}) given the evolved observable O⁡(𝒙,Uℓ)=Uℓ†​(𝒙)​O​Uℓ​(𝒙)O(\bm{x},U_{\ell})=U_{\ell}^{\dagger}(\bm{x})OU_{\ell}(\bm{x}) defined in Eq. (207)-(208) and the upper bound of the related 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}.

Explicit form of fℓ​(𝒙)f_{\ell}(\bm{x}). By construction, the circuit takes the tensor-product form Uℓ​(𝒙)=Wℓ⊗VB​(𝒙)U_{\ell}(\bm{x})=W_{\ell}\otimes V_{B}(\bm{x}) with VB​(𝒙)=∏j=1dRZm+j⁡(𝒙j)​Hm+jV_{B}(\bm{x})=\prod_{j=1}^{d}\RZ_{m+j}(\bm{x}_{j})H_{m+j}, and the observable takes the tensor-product form O=Z1⊗(1d​∑j=1dXm+j)O=Z_{1}\otimes\big(\tfrac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}X_{m+j}\big). Since conjugation preserves tensor products, the evolved observable yields

Uℓ(𝒙)†OUℓ(𝒙)=(Wℓ†Z1Wℓ)⊗1d∑j=1dVB(𝒙)†Xm+jVB(𝒙).U_{\ell}(\bm{x})^{\dagger}O\,U_{\ell}(\bm{x})=\big(W_{\ell}^{\dagger}Z_{1}W_{\ell}\big)\otimes\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}V_{B}(\bm{x})^{\dagger}X_{m+j}V_{B}(\bm{x}). (215)

Because the initial state ρ0=|0⟩​⟨0|⊗N\rho_{0}=\ket{0}\bra{0}^{\otimes N} is also a product state across the same bipartition, the expectation value of the tensor-product operator in Eq. (215) equals the product of the two registers’ expectation values. The first factor is exactly the 𝖡𝖰𝖯\mathsf{BQP} value, i.e., ⟨0m|​Wℓ†​Z1​Wℓ​|0m⟩=μℓ\bra{0^{m}}W_{\ell}^{\dagger}Z_{1}W_{\ell}\ket{0^{m}}=\mu_{\ell}, which is independent of 𝒙\bm{x}. For the second factor, a single-qubit calculation gives

VB​(𝒙)†​Xm+j​VB​(𝒙)=H⁡(cos⁡(𝒙j)​X−sin⁡(𝒙j)​Y)​H=cos⁡(𝒙j)​Zm+j−sin⁡(𝒙j)​Ym+j,V_{B}(\bm{x})^{\dagger}X_{m+j}V_{B}(\bm{x})=H\big(\cos(\bm{x}_{j})\,X-\sin(\bm{x}_{j})\,Y\big)H=\cos(\bm{x}_{j})\,Z_{m+j}-\sin(\bm{x}_{j})\,Y_{m+j}, (216)

so that using ⟨0|​Z​|0⟩=1\bra{0}Z\ket{0}=1 and ⟨0|​Y​|0⟩=0\bra{0}Y\ket{0}=0, its expectation value is 1d​∑j=1dcos⁡(𝒙j)=h⁡(𝒙)\tfrac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\cos(\bm{x}_{j})=h(\bm{x}), which depends only on the input 𝒙\bm{x}. Multiplying the two factors yields fℓ​(𝒙)=μℓ​h​(𝒙)f_{\ell}(\bm{x})=\mu_{\ell}\,h(\bm{x}). Employing the orthogonality relation 𝔼𝒙​cos2⁡(𝒙j)=12\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}}\cos^{2}(\bm{x}_{j})=\tfrac{1}{2} then gives νf=μℓ2​𝔼𝒙​h​(𝒙)2=μℓ2/(2​d)\nu_{f}=\mu_{\ell}^{2}\,\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}}h(\bm{x})^{2}=\mu_{\ell}^{2}/(2d).

𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} bound for O⁡(𝒙,Uℓ)O(\bm{x},U_{\ell}). As shown in Eq. (215), the evolved observable is a sum of single-probe terms, so its trigonometric expansion contains only frequencies of Hamming weight ‖𝝎‖0≤1\|\bm{\omega}\|_{0}\leq 1. Explicitly, its frequency support consists of those modes 𝝎∈{0,±1}d\bm{\omega}\in\{0,\pm 1\}^{d} that are nonzero in exactly one entry, i.e., 𝝎j∈{+1,−1}\bm{\omega}_{j}\in\{+1,-1\} for a single index j∈[d]j\in[d] and 𝝎j′=0\bm{\omega}_{j^{\prime}}=0 for all j′≠jj^{\prime}\neq j. The number of such modes is 2​d2d, since there are dd choices of the index jj and two choices of the sign of 𝝎j\bm{\omega}_{j}. Recall that in the definition of ℳ(α)\mathcal{M}^{(\alpha)} in Eq. (4), a fixed unitary VV maps each operator coefficient as Q𝝎↦V†​Q𝝎​VQ_{\bm{\omega}}\mapsto V^{\dagger}Q_{\bm{\omega}}V but, being independent of 𝒙\bm{x}, leaves the frequency support unchanged. Hence for every fixed VV, the induced distribution p⁡(𝝎)\mathrm{p}(\bm{\omega}) is supported on at most 2​d2d modes, which gives 𝒮(1)​[V†​O​(𝒙,Uℓ)​V]≤log⁡(2​d)\mathcal{S}^{(1)}[V^{\dagger}O(\bm{x};U_{\ell})V]\leq\log(2d) and therefore

ℳ(1)​[O⁡(𝒙,Uℓ)]=maxV⁡𝒮(1)​[V†​O​(𝒙,Uℓ)​V]≤log⁡(2​d).\mathcal{M}^{(1)}[O(\bm{x};U_{\ell})]=\max_{V}\mathcal{S}^{(1)}\big[V^{\dagger}O(\bm{x};U_{\ell})V\big]\leq\log(2d). (217)

This completes the proof. ∎

Proof of Lemma 16.

Since 𝔼𝒙​h​(𝒙)2=1/(2​d)\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}}h(\bm{x})^{2}=1/(2d), the estimator can be rewritten as μ^=𝔼𝒙​[f^​(𝒙)​h​(𝒙)]/𝔼𝒙​[h​(𝒙)2]\hat{\mu}=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}}[\hat{f}(\bm{x})h(\bm{x})]/\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}}[h(\bm{x})^{2}]. Employing the product form fℓ​(𝒙)=μℓ​h​(𝒙)f_{\ell}(\bm{x})=\mu_{\ell}h(\bm{x}) from Lemma 15 and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, we have

|μ^−μℓ|=\displaystyle|\hat{\mu}-\mu_{\ell}|= |𝔼𝒙​[(f^​(𝒙)−μℓ​h​(𝒙))​h​(𝒙)]|𝔼𝒙​[h​(𝒙)2]\displaystyle\frac{\big|\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}}\big[(\hat{f}(\bm{x})-\mu_{\ell}h(\bm{x}))\,h(\bm{x})\big]\big|}{\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}}[h(\bm{x})^{2}]}
≤\displaystyle\leq 𝔼𝒙​(f^​(𝒙)−fℓ​(𝒙))2​𝔼𝒙​[h​(𝒙)2]𝔼𝒙​[h​(𝒙)2]\displaystyle\frac{\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}}(\hat{f}(\bm{x})-f_{\ell}(\bm{x}))^{2}}\,\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}}[h(\bm{x})^{2}]}}{\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}}[h(\bm{x})^{2}]}
=\displaystyle= ϵ𝔼𝒙​[h​(𝒙)2]=2​d​ϵ≤2​d⋅νf16=|μℓ|4,\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{\epsilon}{\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}}[h(\bm{x})^{2}]}}=\sqrt{2d\,\epsilon}\leq\sqrt{2d\cdot\tfrac{\nu_{f}}{16}}=\frac{|\mu_{\ell}|}{4}, (218)

where the second inequality uses the assumption 𝔼𝒙​|f^​(𝒙)−fℓ​(𝒙)|2≤ϵ\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}}|\hat{f}(\bm{x})-f_{\ell}(\bm{x})|^{2}\leq\epsilon, and the last equality follows from νf=μℓ2/(2​d)\nu_{f}=\mu_{\ell}^{2}/(2d). Hence μ^\hat{\mu} and μℓ\mu_{\ell} share the same sign, and |μ^|≥34​|μℓ|≥14|\hat{\mu}|\geq\tfrac{3}{4}|\mu_{\ell}|\geq\tfrac{1}{4} with the last inequality using |μℓ|≥1/3|\mu_{\ell}|\geq 1/3 from Eq. (206).

It remains to bound the cost of estimating μ^\hat{\mu}. Clipping f^​(𝒙)\hat{f}(\bm{x}) to the interval [−1,1][-1,1] never increases the prediction error and ensures that each summand obeys f^​(𝒙)​h​(𝒙)∈[−1,1]\hat{f}(\bm{x})h(\bm{x})\in[-1,1]. Employing Hoeffding’s inequality, a Monte Carlo average over M=𝒪⁡(d2​log⁡(1/δ))M=\mathcal{O}(d^{2}\log(1/\delta)) i.i.d. inputs estimates 𝔼𝒙​[f^​(𝒙)​h​(𝒙)]\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}}[\hat{f}(\bm{x})h(\bm{x})] to an additive accuracy |μℓ|/(16​d)|\mu_{\ell}|/(16d), and hence estimates μ^\hat{\mu} to an accuracy |μℓ|/8|\mu_{\ell}|/8, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta. This completes the proof. ∎

SI I More numerical simulations

This section complements the numerical results presented in the main text with additional implementation details and supporting validation experiments. We first describe the baseline methods considered in the main text and introduce the evaluation metric used throughout our numerical studies in SI. I.1. We then investigate the predictive performance of the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided classical surrogate under finite-shot constraints in SI. I.2. Next, we provide additional numerical evidence for the scalability of the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate in SI. I.3. Finally, in SI. I.4, we demonstrate that the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate improves upon existing classical surrogates with provable efficiency guarantees for pretraining variational quantum algorithms.

I.1 Implementation details of the numerical methods and evaluation metrics

In this section, we elucidate the implementation of the numerical methods and the evaluation metrics used in our experiments. We first describe the learning-based surrogates and classical simulation methods considered in the benchmarks, and then specify the metric used to evaluate their performance.

Classical surrogates and simulators. We consider four numerical methods: the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}}, the Hamming-weight surrogate h𝖼h_{\mathsf{c}}, the matrix-product-state (MPS) simulator, and the Pauli-path simulator (PPS), where the latter two simulators are representative for simulating low-entanglement and low-magic circuits, respectively. Their implementation details are described below.

𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}}. Recall that constructing the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided classical surrogate involves three steps: (i) data collection, (ii) feature selection, and (iii) model construction. In step (i), the classical learner collects a training dataset 𝒯={(𝒙(i),y(i))}i=1n\mathcal{T}=\{(\bm{x}^{(i)},y^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^{n} containing nn examples, where each input 𝒙(i)\bm{x}^{(i)} is independently sampled from the uniform distribution over [−π,π]d[-\pi,\pi]^{d} and y(i)y^{(i)} is a statistical estimation of f⁡(𝒙(i))=Tr⁡(ρ0​U​(𝒙(i))†​O​U​(𝒙(i)))f(\bm{x}^{(i)})=\Tr(\rho_{0}U(\bm{x}^{(i)})^{\dagger}OU(\bm{x}^{(i)})) obtained from mym_{y} measurements. In step (ii), the classical learner selects a subset of features {Φ𝝎​(𝒙)}Λ𝗊\{\Phi_{\bm{\omega}}(\bm{x})\}_{\Lambda_{\mathsf{q}}} from the trigonometric expansion f⁡(𝒙)=∑𝝎∈{0,±1}dΦ𝝎​(𝒙)​Tr⁡(ρ0​Q𝝎)f(\bm{x})=\sum_{\bm{\omega}\in\{0,\pm 1\}^{d}}\Phi_{\bm{\omega}}(\bm{x})\Tr(\rho_{0}Q_{\bm{\omega}}) defined in Eq. (27), where the selected feature set is indexed by Λ𝗊⊂{0,±1}d\Lambda_{\mathsf{q}}\subset\{0,\pm 1\}^{d}. To determine Λ𝗊\Lambda_{\mathsf{q}}, we use the quantum subroutine introduced in SI. F to prepare the 2​d2d-qubit state |ψf⟩=∑𝝎∈{0,±1}dp⁡(𝝎)​|𝝎⟩\ket{\psi_{f}}=\sum_{\bm{\omega}\in\{0,\pm 1\}^{d}}\sqrt{\mathrm{p}(\bm{\omega})}\ket{\bm{\omega}}. The state is measured mfm_{f} times in the computational basis |𝝎⟩​⟨𝝎|\ket{\bm{\omega}}\bra{\bm{\omega}}. The learner then selects the DD most frequently observed modes {𝝎~(i)}i=1D\{\tilde{\bm{\omega}}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{D} and defines Λ𝗊={𝝎~(i)}i=1D\Lambda_{\mathsf{q}}=\{\tilde{\bm{\omega}}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{D}. In the ideal limit mf→∞m_{f}\rightarrow\infty, the selected modes are ordered according to p⁡(𝝎~(1))≥⋯≥p⁡(𝝎~(D))\mathrm{p}(\tilde{\bm{\omega}}^{(1)})\geq\cdots\geq\mathrm{p}(\tilde{\bm{\omega}}^{(D)}).

In step (iii), the learner uses the training dataset 𝒯\mathcal{T} and the selected feature map 𝚽Λ​𝗊\bm{\Phi}_{\Lambda{\mathsf{q}}} to construct the linear surrogate h𝗊​(𝒙,𝐰^)=⟨𝚽Λ𝗊​(𝒙),𝐰^⟩h_{\mathsf{q}}(\bm{x},\hat{\bm{\mathrm{w}}})=\braket{\bm{\Phi}_{\Lambda_{\mathsf{q}}}(\bm{x}),\hat{\bm{\mathrm{w}}}}. The coefficient vector 𝐰^\hat{\bm{\mathrm{w}}} is obtained by solving the ridge-regression problem

𝐰^=arg⁡min⁡∑i=1n𝐰⁡(h𝗊​(𝒙,𝐰)−y(i))2+α​‖𝐰‖,\hat{\bm{\mathrm{w}}}=\arg\min_{\bm{\mathrm{w}}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(h_{\mathsf{q}}(\bm{x},\bm{\mathrm{w}})-y^{(i)}\right)^{2}+\alpha\|\bm{\mathrm{w}}\|, (219)

where α\alpha is the regularization parameter. We set α=1\alpha=1 throughout the numerical experiments.

To distinguish between ideal and finite-shot implementations, we use h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} to denote the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate constructed in the ideal limit my=mf=∞m_{y}=m_{f}=\infty, and h¯𝗊\bar{h}_{\mathsf{q}} to denote the surrogate constructed using finite values of mym_{y} and mfm_{f}. In the numerical comparisons presented below, h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} is primarily used to characterize the predictive capability of the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate under a prescribed inference-time computational budget. Unless explicitly stated otherwise, the one-time cost of constructing h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} during the training stage is not included in the inference-cost comparison.

Hamming-weight surrogate h𝖼h_{\mathsf{c}}. The Hamming-weight surrogate h𝖼h_{\mathsf{c}} is a representative classical surrogate proposed in previous studies and equipped with provable efficiency guarantees [du2025efficient, liao2025demonstration]. Its construction follows the same three-step procedure as that of h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}}, but employs a different feature-selection rule in stage (ii). In particular, the Hamming-weight surrogate has the linear form h𝖼​(𝒙,𝐰^)=⟨𝚽Λ𝖼​(𝒙),𝐰^⟩h_{\mathsf{c}}(\bm{x},\hat{\bm{\mathrm{w}}})=\braket{\bm{\Phi}_{\Lambda_{\mathsf{c}}}(\bm{x}),\hat{\bm{\mathrm{w}}}}, where 𝐰^\hat{\bm{\mathrm{w}}} is obtained using the same ridge-regression procedure described above. The feature vector 𝚽Λ𝖼​(𝒙)\bm{\Phi}_{\Lambda_{\mathsf{c}}}(\bm{x}) is constructed by prioritizing modes 𝝎\bm{\omega} with small Hamming weight ‖𝝎‖0\|\bm{\omega}\|_{0}. For an integer threshold Γ\Gamma, define Λ(Γ)={𝝎∈0,±1d:|𝝎|0≤Γ}\Lambda(\Gamma)=\{\bm{\omega}\in{0,\pm 1}^{d}:|\bm{\omega}|_{0}\leq\Gamma\}. For a prescribed feature budget (D), there may not exist an integer Γ\Gamma satisfying |Λ⁡(Γ)|=D|\Lambda(\Gamma)|=D. We therefore choose Γ′\Gamma^{\prime} such that |Λ⁡(Γ′)|≤D≤|Λ⁡(Γ′+1)||\Lambda(\Gamma^{\prime})|\leq D\leq|\Lambda(\Gamma^{\prime}+1)|. To construct Λ𝖼\Lambda_{\mathsf{c}} of cardinality DD, we include all modes in Λ⁡(Γ′)\Lambda(\Gamma^{\prime}) and then uniformly sample D−|Λ⁡(Γ′)|D-|\Lambda(\Gamma^{\prime})| additional modes from the set {𝝎:‖𝝎‖0=Γ′+1}\{\bm{\omega}:\|\bm{\omega}\|_{0}=\Gamma^{\prime}+1\}. Notably, this feature selection procedure is purely classical and ignores the effect of the structure-dependent quantity Tr⁡(ρ0​Q𝝎)\Tr(\rho_{0}Q_{\bm{\omega}}) in the trigonometric expansion of f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}).

Matrix-product-state simulator. Matrix-product-state methods are tensor-network-based approaches that are particularly effective for simulating quantum circuits whose intermediate states exhibit limited entanglement. To compare h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} with a representative tensor-network simulator, we implement an MPS baseline that independently contracts each parameterized circuit U⁡(𝒙)U(\bm{x}) using the PennyLane tensor-network backend [bergholm2018pennylane].

The maximum MPS bond dimension χ\chi is set equal to the feature dimension DD used by the classical surrogates. This choice provides a controlled comparison between the inference budgets of the learning-based and simulation-based methods. Evaluating a surrogate with DD selected trigonometric features requires at most 𝒪⁡(d​D)\mathcal{O}(dD) arithmetic operations per input when the features are evaluated directly. By contrast, simulating an NN-qubit circuit of depth LL using an MPS generally requires a computational cost that grows at least linearly with N​LNL and polynomially with χ\chi. Consequently, setting χ=D\chi=D ensures that the MPS baseline is not assigned a smaller nominal truncation budget than the surrogate while still reflecting the substantially different computational structures of the two methods.

Pauli-path simulator. As a complementary operator-based simulation method, PPS estimates expectation values f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}) by propagating the measured Pauli observable backward through the circuit in the Heisenberg picture [rudolph2026pauli]. Clifford gates map each Pauli string to a single Pauli string, whereas non-Clifford and parameterized rotation gates can map one Pauli string to a linear combination of multiple Pauli strings. Repeated propagation through such gates therefore produces a branching collection of weighted Pauli paths whose size can grow exponentially with the number of non-Clifford gates.

Different PPS variants control this growth using different truncation strategies. In our implementation, we employ a top-KK truncation rule. After each circuit-layer update, the simulator retains at most the KK Pauli paths with the largest coefficient magnitudes and discards the remaining paths. This truncation keeps the memory and runtime costs explicitly controlled and enables a direct comparison with classical surrogates under a fixed representation budget. The hyperparameter KK specifies the maximum number of Pauli paths retained during propagation. Throughout our numerical comparisons, we set K=DK=D to compare PPS and the predictive surrogates under the same representation budget and to demonstrate the superior predictive performance of h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} over PPS.

Evaluation metric. To evaluate the prediction performance of classical surrogates and simulators under a common criterion, we employ the coefficient of determination (R2R^{2}) on the test dataset {𝒙(i),y(i)}i=1ntest\{\bm{x}^{(i)},y^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{n_{\mathrm{test}}}

R2=1−∑i=1ntest[yi−h⁡(𝒙(i))]2∑i=1ntest(yi−y¯)2,y¯=1ntest​∑i=1ntestyi,R^{2}=1-\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\mathrm{test}}}[y_{i}-h(\bm{x}^{(i)})]^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\mathrm{test}}}(y_{i}-\overline{y})^{2}},\qquad\overline{y}=\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\mathrm{test}}}y_{i}, (220)

where y(i)=Tr⁡[ρ0​U​(𝒙(i))†​O​U​(𝒙(i))]y^{(i)}=\Tr[\rho_{0}U(\bm{x}^{(i)})^{\dagger}OU(\bm{x}^{(i)})] is the exact expectation value and h⁡(𝒙(i))h(\bm{x}^{(i)}) denotes the surrogate prediction or simulator estimate. An ideal predictor achieves R2=1R^{2}=1, while R2=0R^{2}=0 corresponds to the constant predictor y¯\overline{y} (the mean of the test targets). Negative values of R2R^{2} indicate a larger squared prediction error than this constant baseline. Since all negative values represent performance worse than the baseline, we display them as zero in the main-text figures for visualization purposes.

To provide a more nuanced assessment across the full range of prediction accuracy, we also introduce another bounded evaluation metric derived from R2R^{2}, which is given by

R~2=12−R2.\widetilde{R}^{2}=\frac{1}{2-R^{2}}. (221)

Since R~2\widetilde{R}^{2} is a monotonic transformation of R2R^{2}, it preserves the ranking of different methods while mapping the entire range R2∈(−∞,1]R^{2}\in(-\infty,1] onto the normalized interval R~2∈(0,1]\widetilde{R}^{2}\in(0,1]. Consequently, even arbitrarily negative values of R2R^{2} are assigned finite scores within this bounded range, making the metric more suitable for comparing methods with poor predictive performance. Under this definition, exact prediction yields R~2=1\widetilde{R}^{2}=1, the mean predictor gives R~2=1/2\widetilde{R}^{2}=1/2, and values below 1/21/2 indicate performance worse than the mean predictor.

I.2 Numerical results for 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided classical surrogates under finite-shot constraints

The numerical results in the main text are obtained in an idealized setting that neglects the statistical errors arising from a finite number of quantum measurements. In this section, we complement the random-circuit experiments conducted in Fig. 2a by incorporating two distinct sources of measurement error: the finite-shot error in the training labels and the finite-sampling error in identifying the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided features with the quantum subroutine. Treating these two resources separately allows us to distinguish imperfect feature identification from label noise. Specifically, we examine how prediction accuracy varies with the numbers of measurements used for feature identification and label collection, compare practical 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided feature selection with the ideal 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided, Hamming-weight, and random Fourier strategies, and determine how a fixed total measurement budget should be divided between feature identification and training-label collection.

Experimental setting. We consider the random-circuit setting used in Fig. 2a. In particular, the system size is fixed at N=6N=6 with circuit depth L=66L=66. The number of rotation gates and TT gates contained in the circuit U⁡(𝒙)U(\bm{x}) are set as d=6d=6 and Gt=6G_{t}=6, respectively, while CNOT gates are inserted independently with probability γ=0.1\gamma=0.1. For surrogate construction, the training set contains n=100n=100 examples and the feature dimension is fixed at D=8D=8. All surrogates are evaluated on an independent test set of ntest=200n_{\mathrm{test}}=200 examples. We generate three random quantum circuits and perform 2020 independent measurement repetitions for each circuit instance.

To investigate the effect of measurement noise in the training labels, we vary the number of measurements used to estimate each label y(i)y^{(i)} according to

my∈{1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256,512,1024,∞},m_{\mathrm{y}}\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256,512,1024,\infty\}, (222)

where my=∞m_{\mathrm{y}}=\infty denotes exact expectation values. For the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate h¯𝗊\bar{h}_{\mathsf{q}}, we also vary the number of measurements used in the quantum subroutine for feature identification with

mf∈{24,25,…,218}.m_{\mathrm{f}}\in\{2^{4},2^{5},\ldots,2^{18}\}. (223)

Notably, the feature-identification budget mfm_{\mathrm{f}} is required only for constructing h¯𝗊\bar{h}_{\mathsf{q}}. In contrast, the ideal 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} assumes the exact feature-identification, corresponding to the scenario of mf=∞m_{\mathrm{f}}=\infty, while the Hamming-weight surrogate h𝖼h_{\mathsf{c}} and the random Fourier surrogate h𝗋h_{\mathsf{r}} do not require the quantum feature-identification procedure.

For the fixed-budget comparison, we define the total measurement budget as

mt=mf+n⋅my,m_{\mathrm{t}}=m_{\mathrm{f}}+n\cdot m_{\mathrm{y}}, (224)

and consider

mt∈{103,3×103,104,3×104,105,3×105,106}.m_{\mathrm{t}}\in\{10^{3},3\times 10^{3},10^{4},3\times 10^{4},10^{5},3\times 10^{5},10^{6}\}.

For h¯𝗊\bar{h}_{\mathsf{q}}, fractions mf/mt∈{0.05,0.10,0.25,0.50}m_{\mathrm{f}}/m_{\mathrm{t}}\in\{0.05,0.10,0.25,0.50\} are allocated to feature identification, with the remaining budget distributed uniformly across the nn training labels. The Hamming-weight and random Fourier surrogates devote the entire measurement budget to label estimation.

Numerical results. Fig. I.5a first isolates the finite-sampling error arising from feature identification and evaluates the ability of the quantum subroutine to recover important trigonometric features. We quantify the quality of the identified feature set using the captured probability mass

p⁡(Λ𝗊)p⁡(Λ)=∑𝝎∈Λ𝗊p⁡(𝝎)∑𝝎∈{0,±1}p⁡(𝝎),\frac{\mathrm{p}(\Lambda_{\mathsf{q}})}{\mathrm{p}(\Lambda)}=\frac{\sum_{\bm{\omega}\in\Lambda_{\mathsf{q}}}\mathrm{p}(\bm{\omega})}{\sum_{\bm{\omega}\in\{0,\pm 1\}}\mathrm{p}(\bm{\omega})}, (225)

where p⁡(𝝎)=p~​(𝝎)/∑𝝎∈{0,±1}dp~​(𝝎)\mathrm{p}(\bm{\omega})=\tilde{\mathrm{p}}(\bm{\omega})/\sum_{\bm{\omega}\in\{0,\pm 1\}^{d}}\tilde{\mathrm{p}}(\bm{\omega}) with p~​(𝝎)=𝔼𝒙​Φ𝝎​(𝒙)2​Tr⁡(ρ0​Q𝝎)2\tilde{\mathrm{p}}(\bm{\omega})=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}}\Phi_{\bm{\omega}}(\bm{x})^{2}\Tr(\rho_{0}Q_{\bm{\omega}})^{2} is the probability distribution induced by the trigonometric expansion of f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}) in Eq. (77). Here, p⁡(Λ)=1p(\Lambda)=1 and Λ𝗊\Lambda_{\mathsf{q}} denotes the set of distinct modes sampled by employing the quantum subroutine. The results show that increasing the number of feature-identification measurements mfm_{f} substantially improves the recovery of important modes. In particular, the captured probability mass increases from 0.1670.167 at mf=210m_{f}=2^{10} to 0.930.93 at mf=217m_{f}=2^{17}. It reaches unity at mf=218m_{f}=2^{18}, indicating that all modes with nonzero probability, {𝝎:𝗉⁡(𝝎)>0}\{\bm{\omega}:\mathsf{p}(\bm{\omega})>0\}, have been successfully identified. These results demonstrate that the quantum subroutine can reliably recover the important trigonometric features as the measurement budget increases.

Fig. I.5b fixes the feature-identification budget at mf=212m_{f}=2^{12} and varies the number of measurements mym_{y} used to estimate each training label. The predictive performance of all methods improves with mym_{y}, showing that label-estimation noise dominates in the low-shot regime. Nevertheless, the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogates consistently outperform the Hamming-weight and random-feature baselines once mym_{y} is sufficiently large. In particular, with exact training labels, h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} and h¯𝗊\bar{h}_{\mathsf{q}} achieve R~2=1\widetilde{R}^{2}=1 and 0.740.74, respectively, whereas h𝖼h_{\mathsf{c}} and h𝗋h_{\mathsf{r}} remain below 0.50.5. Thus, although mf=212m_{f}=2^{12} does not recover all important modes, the selected features still retain a clear predictive advantage, while the gap between h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} and h¯𝗊\bar{h}_{\mathsf{q}} reflects the cost of imperfect feature identification.

Finally, Fig. I.5c examines how a fixed total measurement budget mtm_{t} should be allocated between feature identification and label estimation. At small mtm_{t}, the additional cost of feature identification can outweigh its benefit, causing the conventional baselines to perform slightly better. As mtm_{t} increases, however, the practical 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate exhibits a clear advantage, with allocating 25%25\%–50%50\% of the budget to feature identification providing the best overall performance. For instance, at mt=104m_{t}=10^{4}, these two allocation strategies achieve R~2=0.62\widetilde{R}^{2}=0.62 and 0.610.61, respectively, compared with 0.440.44 for h𝖼h_{\mathsf{c}} and 0.430.43 for h𝗋h_{\mathsf{r}}. These results show that, once the total measurement budget is sufficient to support both feature and label estimation, the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate substantially outperforms the Hamming-weight and random-feature baselines.

I.3 More numerical results for the scalability of the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided classical surrogates

This subsection complements the scalability analysis in Fig. 3 by further separating the effect of the system sizes and the number of rotation gates, the latter of which controls the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} of the considered circuit. Using the same structured cluster-circuit family, we perform two controlled comparisons. First, we vary NN while keeping 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} fixed to determine whether increasing the system size alone reduces the prediction accuracy. Second, we vary 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} at fixed NN to examine how the prediction accuracy changes as the mode distribution becomes more complex. Together, these experiments test whether the performance of h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} is governed primarily by 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} rather than by the number of qubits. Throughout this analysis, we use the tractable quantity 𝒮(1)\mathcal{S}^{(1)} as a proxy for 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}, denoted by ℳ(1)\mathcal{M}^{(1)}.

Experimental setting. We consider the structured cluster-circuit family introduced in Fig. 3. For the cluster observable with window size k=5k=5, the nonzero modes {𝝎:p⁡(𝝎)>0}\{\bm{\omega}:\mathrm{p}(\bm{\omega})>0\} have equal probabilities p⁡(𝝎)\mathrm{p}(\bm{\omega}) and The number of such modes is

Mnz=(d−k+1)​2k,𝒮(1)=log2⁡Mnz.M_{\mathrm{nz}}=(d-k+1)2^{k},\qquad\mathcal{S}^{(1)}=\log_{2}M_{\mathrm{nz}}. (226)

In the fixed-𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} experiment, we set d=12d=12, for which Mnz=256M_{\mathrm{nz}}=256 and 𝒮(1)=8\mathcal{S}^{(1)}=8, and vary the number of qubits as N∈{20,30,40,50,60,80}N\in\{20,30,40,50,60,80\}. Because increasing NN only adds qubits that do not alter the target function or its mode distribution, both f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}) and p⁡(𝝎)\mathrm{p}(\bm{\omega}) remain unchanged. In the fixed-NN experiment, we set N=40N=40 and vary the number of rotation gates as d∈{6,9,12,15,18,21}d\in\{6,9,12,15,18,21\}, corresponding to 𝒮(1)∈{6.00,7.32,8.00,8.46,8.81,9.09}\mathcal{S}^{(1)}\in\{6.00,7.32,8.00,8.46,8.81,9.09\}.

For both experiments, we consider three combinations of training-set size nn and feature dimension DD, i.e., (n,D)=(100,50),(300,200)(n,D)=(100,50),(300,200), and (500,300)(500,300). When D>MnzD>M_{\mathrm{nz}}, all nonzero modes are retained, and the effective feature dimension is therefore MnzM_{\mathrm{nz}}. Each configuration is averaged over 2020 independently sampled training datasets and evaluated on 10001000 test inputs with exact labels.

Numerical results. As shown in Fig. I.6, the two controlled experiments clearly separate the dependence of the prediction accuracy on 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} from its dependence on the number of qubits. At fixed 𝒮(1)=8\mathcal{S}^{(1)}=8, the performance of h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} exhibits no systematic variation with (N). In particular, for all three choices of (n,D)(n,D), the fitted slopes of the values of R2R^{2} with respect to NN are close to zero. In contrast, at fixed N=40N=40, the accuracy decreases monotonically or near-monotonically as the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} proxy 𝒮(1)\mathcal{S}^{(1)} increases. For example, at (n,D)=(300,200)(n,D)=(300,200), the prediction accuracy R2R^{2} decreases from 11 at 𝒮(1)=6\mathcal{S}^{(1)}=6 to 0.320.32 at 𝒮(1)=8\mathcal{S}^{(1)}=8 and becomes zero for the three largest values of 𝒮(1)\mathcal{S}^{(1)}. At (n,D)=(500,300)(n,D)=(500,300), the model remains exact through 𝒮(1)=8\mathcal{S}^{(1)}=8, where the requested D=300D=300 already contains all 256256 nonzero modes, and then degrades as the mode support {𝝎:p⁡(𝝎)>0}\{\bm{\omega}:\mathrm{p}(\bm{\omega})>0\} grows beyond the feature budget DD. These controlled comparisons show that enlarging NN does not reduce accuracy when the mode distribution p⁡(𝝎)\mathrm{p}(\bm{\omega}) is fixed, whereas increasing 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE} at fixed NN increases the feature and data requirements.

I.4 Application of 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogates: pre-training variational quantum eigensolvers (VQEs)

While the classical surrogates have wide applications as studied in previous studies [du2025efficient, liao2025demonstration], here we focus on a major application of 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogates for enhancing variational quantum algorithms by substantially reducing the quantum resource demands. In the following, we first introduce how to use the classical surrogate to pre-train variational quantum eigensolvers, and then introduce the numerical settings and results.

Implementations of pre-training VQEs with 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided classical surrogate. We first recap the mechanism of VQEs. Given an initial state ρ0\rho_{0} and a target Hamiltonian 𝖧\mathsf{H}, the objective of VQEs is to find the ground state of 𝖧\mathsf{H} by optimizing the following expectation function

min𝒙⁡f⁡(𝒙,𝖧):=min𝒙⁡Tr⁡(ρ0​U​(𝒙)†​𝖧​U​(𝒙)),\min_{\bm{x}}f(\bm{x},\mathsf{H}):=\min_{\bm{x}}\Tr(\rho_{0}U(\bm{x})^{\dagger}\mathsf{H}U(\bm{x})), (227)

where U⁡(𝒙)U(\bm{x}) is a variation quantum circuits. To achieve this, a common strategy is to use a gradient descent optimizer to iteratively update the tunable parameters 𝒙\bm{x} to minimize f⁡(𝒙,𝖧)f(\bm{x},\mathsf{H}). Specifically, at the tt-th iteration, the updating rule yields

𝒙(t+1)=𝒙(t)−η​∇𝒙f​(𝒙(t),𝖧),\bm{x}^{(t+1)}=\bm{x}^{(t)}-\eta\nabla_{\bm{x}}f(\bm{x}^{(t)},\mathsf{H}), (228)

where η\eta is the learning rate. This process continues until the loss function converges to a predefined condition. However, implementing VQEs on quantum processors incurs significant measurement overhead, primarily due to the need for estimating expectation values and gradients during the optimization process. As indicated in previous studies [du2025efficient, liao2025demonstration], a well-optimized classical surrogate h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} can alleviate the expensive measurement overhead via pre-training. Instead of directly optimizing f⁡(𝒙(t),𝖧)f(\bm{x}^{(t)},\mathsf{H}), the target parameters can be obtained by minimizing h𝗊​(𝒙,𝖧)h_{\mathsf{q}}(\bm{x},\mathsf{H}), i.e.,

min𝒙⁡h𝗊​(𝒙,𝖧)\min_{\bm{x}}h_{\mathsf{q}}(\bm{x},\mathsf{H}) (229)

This process is entirely classical and does not involve any access to quantum processors. Given access to the optimized 𝒙^\hat{\bm{x}}, one can further minimize f⁡(𝒙^,𝖧)f(\hat{\bm{x}},\mathsf{H}) on quantum devices for additional fine-tuning.

Experimental settings. Here, we consider the 1D open-boundary transverse field Ising models (TFIMs), with the formal expression as

𝖧=−∑i=1N−1ZiZi+1−∑i=1NXi.\mathsf{H}=-\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}Z_{i}Z_{i+1}-\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_{i}. (230)

The initial state is ρ0=|0⟩​⟨0|⊗N\rho_{0}=\ket{0}\bra{0}^{\otimes N} and the adopted ansatz in VQE employs the Hardware efficient ansatz of the form

U⁡(𝒙)=∏ℓ=1L[∏i=1N−1CNOT⁡∏i=1Ni,i+1⁡RY⁡(𝒙ℓ,i)]U(\bm{x})=\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}\left[\prod_{i=1}^{N-1}\CNOT_{i,i+1}\prod_{i=1}^{N}\mathrm{RY}(\bm{x}_{\ell,i})\right] (231)

where the input dimension is d=L​Nd=LN.

The TFIM considered here is set to N=6N=6, J=g=1J=g=1. The circuit depth of U⁡(𝒙)U(\bm{x}) is set as L=2L=2. For the construction of h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}}, the training data size and the feature dimension is set as

n∈{50,100,200,400,1600},D∈{8,16,32,128,512}.n\in\{50,100,200,400,1600\},\qquad D\in\{8,16,32,128,512\}. (232)

The total budget of measurement for constructing surrogates is set as

mt∈{28,210,212,214,216}.m_{t}\in\{2^{8},2^{10},2^{12},2^{14},2^{16}\}. (233)

For the optimization of VQEs, all methods start from the same initial parameter point, and we use Adam [kingma2017adam] as the optimizer with learning rate 0.080.08. To examine the ability of the optimized surrogate hh in estimating the ground state energy, we use the normalized deviation as a metric to quantify its performance

ℜ⁡(𝒙)=|f⁡(𝒙)−E0|Emax−E0,\mathfrak{R}(\bm{x})=\frac{\left|f(\bm{x})-E_{0}\right|}{E_{\max}-E_{0}}, (234)

where E0E_{0} and EmaxE_{\max} are the minimum and maximum eigenvalues of 𝖧\mathsf{H}.

Numerical results. Figure I.7a presents the prediction performance R~2=(2−R2)−1\widetilde{R}^{2}=(2-R^{2})^{-1} of the ideal 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} and Hamming-weight surrogate h𝖼h_{\mathsf{c}} across different feature dimensions DD and training-set sizes nn. The 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate achieves strong predictive performance with only moderate resources, namely h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} reaches R~2=0.87\widetilde{R}^{2}=0.87 using D=32D=32 and n=50n=50. By contrast, even with D=512D=512 and n=1600n=1600, h𝖼h_{\mathsf{c}} remains below R~2=0.5\widetilde{R}^{2}=0.5, indicating performance worse than the mean predictor. These results demonstrate the superior performance of h𝗊h_{\mathsf{q}} over h𝖼h_{\mathsf{c}} and highlight the importance of identifying the most relevant features when constructing predictive surrogates.

Figure I.7b further examines whether this advantage persists when feature identification and training-label estimation share a fixed total measurement budget. With 25%25\% of the budget allocated to feature identification, the performance of the finite-shot surrogate h¯𝗊\bar{h}_{\mathsf{q}} improves from R~2=0.41\widetilde{R}^{2}=0.41 at mt=28m_{t}=2^{8} to 0.930.93 at mt=216m_{t}=2^{16}. At the largest budget mt=218m_{t}=2^{18}, h𝖼h_{\mathsf{c}} reaches only 0.300.30 with n=50n=50 and 0.460.46 with n=200n=200. Thus, although increasing the number of training samples improves h𝖼h_{\mathsf{c}}, it does not recover the advantage obtained by allocating part of the measurement budget to 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided feature identification.

Finally, we examine whether the prediction advantage of the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate translates into improved VQE optimization. As shown in Fig. I.7(c), increasing mfm_{f} from 282^{8} to 2122^{12} improves the test accuracy of h¯𝗊\bar{h}_{\mathsf{q}} from 0.5610.561 to 0.8980.898. Correspondingly, the normalized energy error after 80 classical pre-training iterations decreases from ℜ=0.279\mathfrak{R}=0.279 to 0.0440.044. By contrast, pre-training with h𝖼h_{\mathsf{c}} yields ℜ=0.506\mathfrak{R}=0.506, providing a substantially less effective initialization. We then fine-tune the pre-trained parameters by optimizing the circuit objective ff for 20 additional iterations. The final errors are 0.0700.070, 0.0360.036, and 0.0260.026 for mf=28m_{f}=2^{8}, 2102^{10}, and 2122^{12}, respectively, compared with 0.1710.171 for h𝖼h_{\mathsf{c}}. In particular, the mf=212m_{f}=2^{12} protocol approaches the accuracy of directly optimizing ff for 100 iterations, which yields ℜ=0.024\mathfrak{R}=0.024.

We further compare the quantum measurement costs of these two procedures. The ansatz contains d=12d=12 independent parameters, so the parameter-shift rule requires 2​d=242d=24 energy evaluations per gradient step. With my=64m_{y}=64 measurements per energy evaluation, direct optimization for 100 iterations requires 100​(2​d)​my=153,600100(2d)m_{y}=153{,}600 circuit executions. The 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided protocol instead requires mf+n​my=10,496m_{f}+nm_{y}=10{,}496 executions to construct the surrogate at mf=212m_{f}=2^{12} and n=100n=100, followed by 20​(2​d)​my=30,72020(2d)m_{y}=30{,}720 executions for circuit fine-tuning. Its total measurement cost is therefore 41,21641{,}216, while the preceding 80 surrogate-optimization iterations are performed entirely classically. Under this parameter-shift accounting, 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided pre-training reduces the total quantum measurement cost by 73.2%73.2\%, while attaining nearly the same ground-state accuracy as direct VQE optimization. Together, these results show that the improved landscape approximation enabled by the 𝖣𝖲𝖤\mathsf{DSE}-guided surrogate provides a high-quality initialization and substantially reduces the quantum measurement cost required for VQE optimization.
